lessons.title: Parts of speech

scenes.text: In Hyderabad, Farhan's English teacher Mrs Pinto writes one sentence on the board: “The clever cat quickly jumped onto the old wall, and wow, it never fell!”
She gives each team a job card: Noun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Pronoun, Preposition, Conjunction, Interjection.
Farhan's team finds every word's job. 'Grammar isn't a list of rules,' he says, 'it's knowing what job each word is doing.'

steps.title: Nouns and pronouns
steps.body:
**Noun** — a naming word for a person, place, thing or idea.
- **Common:** girl, city, river · **Proper:** Priya, Kolkata, Ganga (capital letter!)
- **Collective:** a **team** of players, a **flock** of birds, a **bunch** of grapes
- **Abstract:** honesty, happiness, freedom (ideas you can't touch)
- **Countable** (one book, two books) vs **uncountable** (water, advice, furniture, information)

**Pronoun** — replaces a noun to avoid repetition: I, you, he, she, it, we, they; me, him, her, us, them; my, mine, your, yours; myself; who, which, that.

steps.title: Verbs
steps.body:
A **verb** shows an action (run, write, think) or a state (is, seem, belong).
- **Main verbs** carry the meaning: She **plays**.
- **Helping (auxiliary) verbs** support them: be (am/is/are/was/were), have (has/had), do (does/did).
- **Modals** add ideas like ability or duty: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must. After a modal, use the **base form**: She **can swim** (not *can swims*).

**Transitive** verbs need an object (She **kicked** the ball); **intransitive** verbs don't (The baby **slept**).

steps.title: Adjectives and adverbs
steps.body:
**Adjective** — describes a noun: a **tall** tree, **three** mangoes, **this** bag.
Degrees: tall → tall**er** → tall**est**; beautiful → **more** beautiful → **most** beautiful; irregular: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

**Adverb** — describes a verb, adjective or another adverb: how, when, where, how often.
- She sings **beautifully** (how). We left **early** (when). Come **here** (where). He **always** smiles (how often). It's **very** cold (degree).
- Many adverbs end in **-ly**, but not all (fast, hard, well).

**Good** is an adjective; **well** is usually the adverb: She is a **good** singer; she sings **well**.

steps.title: Prepositions, conjunctions, interjections
steps.body:
**Preposition** — shows the relation of a noun to other words, often place or time: in, on, at, under, between, among, since, for, by, with.

**Conjunction** — joins words or clauses: and, but, or, so, because, although, when, if, while.

**Interjection** — expresses sudden feeling: Wow! Oh! Ouch! Hurray! Alas!

**Key idea:** the same word can be different parts of speech. 'I **light** the lamp' (verb); 'The **light** is bright' (noun); 'a **light** bag' (adjective).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *Informations, advices, furnitures* ✗ — these are uncountable: **information, advice, furniture**.
- *He can sings* ✗ → **He can sing**.
- *She did a good work* ✗ → **She did good work** / **She did a good job**.
- *More better* ✗ → **better**.
- *Me and Ravi went* → better: **Ravi and I went** (subject) / 'with **Ravi and me**' (object).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Label every word: 'Oh! The tired farmer slowly walked home because it was raining heavily.'

*Answer:* Oh (interjection), The (article/determiner), tired (adjective), farmer (noun), slowly (adverb), walked (verb), home (adverb), because (conjunction), it (pronoun), was raining (verb), heavily (adverb).

activity.prompt: Sort the words by part of speech.

quiz.q: In 'a swarm of bees', swarm is a
quiz.why: A collective noun names a group of things taken together. 'Swarm' names a group of bees, like 'herd' or 'team'.

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.why: A modal verb like 'can' is followed by the base form of the verb, with no 's' and no 'to'. So 'She can dance' is correct.

quiz.q: In 'He runs fast', fast is an
quiz.why: In 'He runs fast', 'fast' tells how he runs, so it is an adverb. An adjective would describe a noun, like 'a fast runner'.

quiz.q: Which word is uncountable?
quiz.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, so we say 'some advice' and not 'two advices'. Chair, pencil and idea can be counted.

quiz.q: Choose the correct one: 'She sings ___.'
quiz.why: 'Sings' is a verb, so it needs an adverb to describe how she sings. 'Well' is the adverb; 'good' is an adjective and 'goodly' is not used this way.

lessons.title: Tenses made simple

scenes.text: Jia in Shillong keeps a diary. On Monday she wrote: “I play football every day. Yesterday I scored a goal. Tomorrow I will play the final.”
Her friend Tenzing reads it and asks why she wrote 'I have been practising for weeks' and not 'I practise for weeks'.
Jia explains: tenses aren't just past, present and future — they also show whether an action is simple, continuing, completed, or completed-but-continuing. Twelve tenses, one simple pattern.

steps.title: The 3 × 4 pattern
steps.body:
Each **time** (present, past, future) has four **aspects**:
- **Simple** — facts, habits, completed events
- **Continuous** (progressive) — action in progress: be + **-ing**
- **Perfect** — completed before a point: have/has/had + **past participle**
- **Perfect continuous** — started earlier and continuing up to a point: have/has/had **been** + **-ing**

Master the pattern and you can build all twelve.

steps.title: Present tenses
steps.body:
- **Simple present:** habits, facts, timetables. *She **walks** to school. Water **boils** at 100 °C. The train **leaves** at 6.* (Add **-s/-es** for he/she/it.)
- **Present continuous:** now, or temporary. *I **am reading** now. They **are staying** with us this week.*
- **Present perfect:** past action with a link to now; no exact past time. *I **have finished** my homework. She **has visited** Agra twice.*
- **Present perfect continuous:** started in the past and still going. *We **have been waiting** for two hours.*

With **since** (point of time) and **for** (length of time): *since 2020*, *for three years*.

steps.title: Past and future tenses
steps.body:
**Past:**
- Simple: *He **played** yesterday.* (irregular: go → **went**, see → **saw**, write → **wrote**)
- Continuous: *I **was sleeping** when the phone rang.*
- Perfect: *The film **had started** before we arrived.* (the earlier of two past actions)
- Perfect continuous: *She **had been studying** for hours before the power went off.*

**Future:**
- Simple: *I **will call** you.* · Plans: *I **am going to** learn guitar.*
- Continuous: *At 8 p.m. I **will be travelling**.*
- Perfect: *By June, she **will have finished** the course.*
- Perfect continuous: *By December, I **will have been working** here for a year.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *I am knowing him* ✗ → **I know him**. 'State' verbs (know, like, love, want, believe, belong, understand) are rarely used in continuous form.
- *I have seen him yesterday* ✗ → **I saw him yesterday** (exact past time → simple past).
- *I am living here since 2019* ✗ → **I have been living / have lived here since 2019**.
- *He don't like it* ✗ → **He doesn't like it**.
- *Did you went?* ✗ → **Did you go?** (after did, use the base form).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Fill with the correct form of the verb in brackets:
1. Look! It ___ (rain).
2. She ___ (live) in Delhi since 2015.
3. When I reached the station, the train ___ already ___ (leave).
4. Next year we ___ (visit) Kerala.

*Answers:* 1) is raining 2) has lived / has been living 3) had … left 4) will visit / are going to visit

activity.prompt: Write the correct verb form.
activity.text: Every morning Ravi ___ (drink) milk. Right now he ___ (watch) cricket. Yesterday he ___ (go) to the market. He ___ (live) in Pune since 2020.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have meet her last week.
I have met her last week.
I am meeting her last week.
quiz.why: 'Last week' is a finished, definite time in the past, so the simple past 'met' is needed. The present perfect cannot be used with a specific past time.

quiz.q: 'They ___ football when it started raining.'
quiz.why: The playing was in progress when the rain started and interrupted it, so the past continuous 'were playing' is used.

quiz.q: 'She has been learning Kathak ___ five years.'
quiz.why: 'For' is used with a length of time (five years), while 'since' is used with a starting point such as 2019.

quiz.q: By the time we arrived, the show ___.
quiz.why: The show began before we arrived, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect: 'had begun'.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.why: With 'he', the negative helper is 'doesn't', and the main verb stays in its base form. So 'knows' after 'doesn't' is wrong, and 'don't' does not agree with 'he'.

lessons.title: Subject–verb agreement

story.title: The news headline that went wrong

scenes.text: Kavin edits his school newspaper in Coimbatore. A headline reads: “The team are winning, and each of the players have trained hard.”
The editor, Ms Dsouza, circles 'have'. 'Each is singular — each one has.'
Kavin fixes it: “Each of the players has trained hard.” He learns that the verb must agree with its real subject, not with the nearest noun.

steps.title: The basic rule
steps.body:
A **singular subject takes a singular verb**; a **plural subject takes a plural verb**.
- The boy **runs**. The boys **run**.
- She **is** happy. They **are** happy.
- He **has** a cycle. They **have** cycles.

In the simple present, the singular verb usually ends in **-s** — the opposite of nouns!

steps.title: Find the real subject
steps.body:
Ignore phrases between the subject and the verb:
- The **box** of chocolates **is** on the table. (box, not chocolates)
- One **of my friends** → **One** of my friends **lives** in Paris.
- The **teacher**, along with her students, **is** coming. ('along with', 'as well as', 'together with' don't make the subject plural)

steps.title: Tricky cases
steps.body:
- **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody** → singular: *Everyone **is** here. Neither answer **is** correct.*
- **A and B** → plural: *Ram and Shyam **are** friends.* (But a single idea: *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast.*)
- **Either…or / Neither…nor** → the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: *Neither the teacher nor the **students were** late. Either the students or the **teacher is** coming.*
- **Uncountable nouns** → singular: *The information **is** useful.*
- **Amounts as one unit** → singular: *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk. Five hundred rupees **is** enough.*
- **Plural-looking but singular:** *Mathematics **is** fun. The news **is** good.*
- **Always plural:** scissors, trousers, spectacles: *My scissors **are** blunt.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *One of the boys are absent* ✗ → **is**.
- *Everybody have finished* ✗ → **has**.
- *The news are shocking* ✗ → **is**.
- *There is many people* ✗ → **There are many people** (the subject comes after 'there').

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Choose the verb:
1. The quality of the mangoes (is/are) excellent.
2. Neither Asha nor her brothers (was/were) at home.
3. Physics (is/are) my favourite subject.

*Answers:* 1) is 2) were 3) is

statements.s: ‘Each of the students has a book.’ is correct.
statements.why: Each is singular → has.

statements.s: ‘The news are good today.’ is correct.
statements.why: News is singular: the news is good.

statements.s: ‘My trousers are torn.’ is correct.
statements.why: Trousers is always plural.

statements.s: ‘There is many birds on the tree.’ is correct.
statements.why: Many birds is plural: there are.

statements.s: ‘Neither the coach nor the players were ready.’ is correct.
statements.why: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, players.

quiz.q: The bag of apples ___ heavy.
quiz.why: The subject is 'bag', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'. 'Of apples' only describes the bag.

quiz.q: Either my parents or my sister ___ coming.
quiz.why: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Sister' is singular, so it is 'is'.

quiz.q: Mathematics ___ my strongest subject.
quiz.why: 'Mathematics' looks plural but is a singular subject, so it takes 'is'. Other subject names like physics work the same way.

quiz.q: The principal, as well as the teachers, ___ present.
quiz.why: 'As well as' does not make the subject plural. The subject is 'the principal', which is singular, so 'was' agrees with it.

lessons.title: Articles, determiners and prepositions

story.title: Maya's message to her host family

scenes.text: Maya from Bhubaneswar goes on a school exchange to Melbourne. She messages her host family: “I will reach at airport in the evening of Monday. I am bringing an useful gift.”
Her host, Mrs Clarke, kindly replies: “We'll meet you at the airport on Monday evening! What's the useful gift?”
Maya notices three small differences: 'at the airport', 'on Monday evening', 'a useful'. Tiny words — but they make English sound natural.

steps.title: A, an and the
steps.body:
**A / an** — one of many, mentioned for the first time (singular countable nouns).
- Use **a** before a consonant **sound**: a book, a **u**niversity (you-), a **o**ne-rupee coin (wun-)
- Use **an** before a vowel **sound**: an apple, an **h**our (silent h), an **M**LA (em-), an honest man

**The** — a specific thing both speakers know, or the only one: *the Sun, the Himalayas, the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Taj Mahal, the best student, the first day.*

**No article** with most names of people, cities and countries, languages, meals and general uncountable/plural ideas: *Delhi, Hindi, lunch, Honesty is important, Dogs are loyal.* (But *the USA, the UK, the Netherlands*.)

steps.title: Determiners: some, any, much, many, few, little
steps.body:
- **Some** — positive sentences and offers: *I have some money. Would you like some tea?*
- **Any** — negatives and questions: *I don't have any money. Do you have any questions?*
- **Many / few / a few** — countable: *many books, few friends (almost none), a few friends (some)*
- **Much / little / a little** — uncountable: *much water, little time (almost none), a little time (some)*
- **Each / every** + singular noun; **both** + plural; **either / neither** + singular.

steps.title: Prepositions of time and place
steps.body:
**Time:**
- **at** + clock time, night, festivals as moments: *at 6 o'clock, at night, at noon*
- **on** + days and dates: *on Monday, on 15 August, on my birthday*
- **in** + months, years, seasons, parts of the day: *in May, in 2025, in winter, in the morning*
- **since** (point) / **for** (duration): *since Monday, for two days*

**Place:**
- **at** a point: *at the bus stop, at the door, at school*
- **on** a surface: *on the table, on the wall*
- **in** inside/area: *in the box, in Chennai, in the garden*
- **between** two; **among** more than two

**Fixed phrases:** *good **at** maths, interested **in** music, afraid **of** the dark, depend **on**, married **to**, discuss **something** (no 'about'), reach Delhi (no 'at')*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *an useful* ✗ → **a useful** (you- sound)
- *a hour* ✗ → **an hour**
- *reach at home / reach to Delhi* ✗ → **reach home / reach Delhi**
- *discuss about the plan* ✗ → **discuss the plan**
- *I am going to the bed* ✗ → **going to bed**
- *since two hours* ✗ → **for two hours**
- *He is the my friend* ✗ → **He is my friend**

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Fill in a/an/the/no article:
1. She is ___ engineer.
2. ___ Moon looks bright tonight.
3. I had ___ lunch at noon.
4. He waited ___ an hour (for/since).

*Answers:* 1) an 2) The 3) no article 4) for

activity.prompt: Fill in the missing article or preposition.
activity.text: I was born ___ 2013 ___ a small town. My exam is ___ Monday ___ 9 a.m. It is ___ honour to meet you.

quiz.q: ___ European tourist asked for directions.
quiz.why: 'European' starts with a 'you' sound, a consonant sound, so we use 'a', not 'an'. The choice depends on sound, not spelling.

quiz.q: We will meet ___ Friday.
quiz.why: We use 'on' before days of the week, as in 'on Friday'. 'At' is for clock times and 'in' for months and years.

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.why: 'Discuss' takes a direct object without a preposition. So 'discussed the trip' is correct, and 'discussed about' is a common mistake.

quiz.q: There is ___ milk left — just enough for one cup.
quiz.why: Milk is uncountable, and 'a little' means some but not much, which fits 'just enough for one cup'. 'Few' and 'many' go with countable nouns.

quiz.q: Share the sweets ___ all five children.
quiz.why: 'Among' is used for more than two people or things, here five children. 'Between' is for two.

sources: Standard English grammar (topic reference)

questions.q: 'Honesty' is a/an
questions.why: 'Honesty' names a quality or idea that cannot be touched, so it is an abstract noun. Proper nouns are names of particular people or places.

questions.q: I ___ to school every day.
questions.why: With 'I' and a habit, the verb is the base form, 'go'. 'Goes' is used with he, she and it.

questions.q: She is ___ honest girl.
questions.why: The 'h' in 'honest' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'.

questions.q: In 'They laughed loudly', loudly is an
questions.why: 'Loudly' tells how they laughed, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb. Adjectives describe nouns.

questions.q: Look! The baby ___.
questions.why: 'Look!' points to something happening now, so the present continuous 'is sleeping' fits.

questions.q: Everyone ___ invited.
questions.why: 'Everyone' is singular, so it takes a singular verb: 'is invited'.

questions.q: I ___ him since childhood.
questions.why: 'Since childhood' shows an action that started in the past and continues now, which takes the present perfect. 'Know' is a state verb, so it is not used in the continuous form.

questions.q: Which is correct?
questions.why: 'Information' is uncountable, so it has no plural and cannot take 'a' or 'an'. We say 'some information'.

questions.q: The flowers in the vase ___ fresh.
questions.why: The subject is 'flowers', which is plural, so the verb is 'are'. 'In the vase' does not change the subject.

questions.q: When I reached the hall, the speech ___.
questions.why: The speech ended before I reached the hall, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect: 'had already ended'.

questions.q: Neither the players nor the coach ___ happy with the result.
questions.why: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Coach' is singular, so it is 'was'.

questions.q: By next March, Leela ___ in this school for five years.
questions.why: The sentence looks ahead to next March and shows how long she will have studied by then, so we use the future perfect continuous: 'will have been studying'.

questions.q: Choose the error-free sentence.
options: He reached the station on time.
He reach the station on time.
He reached to the station in time of.
He reached at the station on time.
questions.why: 'Reach' is a transitive verb and takes no preposition, so 'reached the station' is correct. 'On time' means punctually.

lessons.title: Sentences and clauses

scenes.text: Tanvi in Indore writes an essay where every sentence is short: “I woke up. I was late. I ran. I missed the bus.”
Then she tries one long sentence joined only with 'and': “I woke up and I was late and I ran and I missed the bus and…”
Her teacher Mr Fernandes shows her how to mix: “Because I woke up late, I ran to the stop, but I still missed the bus.” Same events — now the reader feels the story.

steps.title: Subject, predicate and clauses
steps.body:
A **sentence** expresses a complete thought, has a **subject** (who/what) and a **predicate** (what is said about it), and begins with a capital letter.
*[The old man] [planted a mango tree.]*

**Four kinds by purpose:** statement (.), question (?), command/request (.), exclamation (!).

A **clause** is a group of words with a subject and a verb.
- **Main (independent) clause** — makes sense alone: *I stayed home*
- **Subordinate (dependent) clause** — can't stand alone: *because it was raining*

A **phrase** has no subject–verb pair: *in the morning, under the bridge*.

steps.title: Simple, compound and complex
steps.body:
- **Simple:** one main clause. *Aman plays the tabla.*
- **Compound:** two main clauses joined by a **coordinating conjunction** — **FANBOYS**: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. *Aman plays the tabla, **and** his sister sings.*
- **Complex:** a main clause + one or more subordinate clauses, joined by **subordinating conjunctions** (because, although, when, if, unless, since, while, after, before) or **relative pronouns** (who, which, that, whose). *Aman practises daily **because** he has a concert.* / *The girl **who sings** is his sister.*

Tip: if the subordinate clause comes first, put a **comma** after it: *Although it was late, we kept going.*

steps.title: Relative clauses and conditionals
steps.body:
**Relative clauses** add information about a noun:
- **who** for people, **which** for things, **that** for people or things, **whose** for possession, **where** for places.
*The book **that I borrowed** is overdue. My uncle, **who lives in Goa**, is a fisherman.*

**Conditionals (if-clauses):**
- **Zero** (facts): *If you heat ice, it melts.*
- **First** (real future): *If it rains, we **will** stay in.*
- **Second** (unreal present/future): *If I **had** wings, I **would** fly.*
- (Third — unreal past — you'll meet later: *If I had studied, I would have passed.*)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Fragments:** *Because I was tired.* ✗ (no main clause) → *I slept early because I was tired.*
- **Run-ons / comma splices:** *It was late, we went home* ✗ → *It was late, so we went home.* / *It was late; we went home.*
- Doubling conjunctions: *Although it rained, but we played* ✗ → drop 'but'.
- *If it will rain, …* ✗ → **If it rains, …** (no 'will' in the if-clause of a first conditional).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Combine into one good sentence:
1. The shop was closed. We went home. (use 'so')
2. She was ill. She went to school. (use 'although')
3. I met a boy. He can speak five languages. (use 'who')

*Answers:* 1) The shop was closed, so we went home. 2) Although she was ill, she went to school. 3) I met a boy who can speak five languages.

activity.prompt: Simple, compound or complex sentence?

items.text: I called him, but he didn't answer.
When the bell rang, everyone ran out.
She studied hard, so she passed.
The phone that I bought is broken.

quiz.q: 'Because the road was flooded' is a
quiz.why: 'Because the road was flooded' has a subject and verb but does not make complete sense alone, so it is a subordinate clause. It needs a main clause.

quiz.q: Which is a compound sentence?
options: The tea that you made is great.
When I wake up, I drink tea.
I like tea, but my brother likes coffee.
quiz.why: A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a conjunction like 'but'. 'I like tea' and 'my brother likes coffee' can each stand alone.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He was rich although but unhappy.
Although he was rich he but unhappy.
Although he was rich, he was unhappy.
Although he was rich, but he was unhappy.
quiz.why: 'Although' and 'but' both show contrast, so they should not be used together. 'Although he was rich, he was unhappy' is correct.

quiz.q: 'If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.'
quiz.why: In a first conditional the 'if' clause uses the simple present and the main clause uses 'will'. So 'if it rains' is correct.

quiz.q: Which relative pronoun fits? 'This is the girl ___ bag was stolen.'
quiz.why: 'Whose' shows possession and joins the clause 'bag was stolen' to 'girl'. 'Who' would not be followed by 'bag'.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice

scenes.text: At a school in Guwahati, a window is found broken. The notice says: “The window was broken during lunch break.”
Arpit says, 'The notice doesn't tell us who broke it!' Then Riddhi admits: “I broke the window while playing cricket. I'm sorry.”
Their teacher praises Riddhi's honesty — and uses it to show the class the difference between passive voice (focus on the action) and active voice (focus on the doer).

steps.title: What voice means
steps.body:
**Active voice:** the subject **does** the action. *Riddhi **broke** the window.*
**Passive voice:** the subject **receives** the action. *The window **was broken** (by Riddhi).*

**Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle** (broken, written, made, sent).

Only verbs with an **object** (transitive verbs) can become passive. *She slept* has no passive.

steps.title: Changing active to passive
steps.body:
1. Make the **object** the new subject.
2. Use the correct form of **be** in the **same tense** + past participle.
3. Put the old subject after **by** (or leave it out if it is unknown or unimportant).

| Tense | Active | Passive |
- Simple present: *She **writes** a letter.* → *A letter **is written** by her.*
- Present continuous: *They **are building** a bridge.* → *A bridge **is being built**.*
- Present perfect: *He **has finished** the work.* → *The work **has been finished**.*
- Simple past: *Ravi **painted** the wall.* → *The wall **was painted** by Ravi.*
- Future: *They **will announce** the results.* → *The results **will be announced**.*
- Modal: *You **must complete** the form.* → *The form **must be completed**.*

Pronouns change: I → me, he → him, they → them after 'by'.

steps.title: When to use which
steps.body:
**Active** is usually clearer and more direct — prefer it in stories and most writing.

**Passive** is useful when:
- the doer is unknown: *My bicycle **was stolen**.*
- the doer is obvious or unimportant: *Rice **is grown** in Punjab.*
- you're writing science reports or notices: *The solution **was heated** for 5 minutes. Visitors **are requested** to sign in.*

Be alert: the passive can be used to **hide responsibility** ('Mistakes were made').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the tense: *He wrote a poem* → *A poem is written by him* ✗ → **was written**.
- Wrong participle: *The song was sang* ✗ → **sung**; *The letter was wrote* ✗ → **written**.
- Forgetting 'being' in continuous: *The house is built now* (means it's finished) vs *The house is being built* (in progress).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Change the voice:
1. The chef cooked a delicious meal.
2. The students are planting trees.
3. Someone has stolen my wallet.

*Answers:* 1) A delicious meal was cooked by the chef. 2) Trees are being planted by the students. 3) My wallet has been stolen.

activity.prompt: Match each active sentence to its passive form.
pairs: A song is sung by her.
A song was sung by her.
A song is being sung by her.
A song has been sung by her.
A song will be sung by her.

quiz.q: Passive of 'The dog chased the cat':
options: The dog was chased by the cat.
The cat is chased by the dog.
The cat was chased by the dog.
quiz.why: In the passive, the object becomes the subject: 'the cat'. The simple past 'chased' becomes 'was chased by'. The other options change the meaning or tense.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in passive voice?
options: A story was written by Meena.
quiz.why: Passive voice uses be + past participle, and the subject receives the action. 'A story was written by Meena' is passive; the others are active.

quiz.q: Passive of 'They are repairing the road':
quiz.why: The present continuous 'are repairing' becomes 'is being repaired' in the passive. 'Being' keeps the action in progress.

quiz.q: Which sentence CANNOT be made passive?
quiz.why: Only sentences with an object can become passive. 'The baby slept' has no object, so it cannot be made passive.

lessons.title: Direct and reported speech

scenes.text: In Chandigarh, Nikhil's cricket coach, Mr Sandhu, tells him: “You are playing in the final tomorrow.”
Nikhil runs home and says to his mother: “Coach said that I was playing in the final the next day!”
His mother laughs: 'You changed are to was and tomorrow to the next day without even thinking. That's reported speech!'

steps.title: Direct vs reported
steps.body:
**Direct speech** gives the speaker's **exact words** inside quotation marks:
*Asha said, “I am tired.”*

**Reported (indirect) speech** reports the meaning without quotation marks, usually with **that**:
*Asha said that she **was** tired.*

Three things usually change: **pronouns**, **tense** (if the reporting verb is in the past) and **time/place words**.

steps.title: The backshift of tenses
steps.body:
When the reporting verb is past (*said, told*), move the tense **one step back**:
- am/is → **was**; are → **were**
- present simple (play) → **past simple (played)**
- present continuous (is playing) → **past continuous (was playing)**
- present perfect (has played) → **past perfect (had played)**
- past simple (played) → **past perfect (had played)**
- will → **would**; can → **could**; may → **might**; shall → should

**No change** if the reporting verb is present (*He says that he is tired*) or for **universal truths** (*The teacher said that the Earth **goes** round the Sun*).

steps.title: Time and place words
steps.body:
- now → **then**
- today → **that day**
- tomorrow → **the next day / the following day**
- yesterday → **the day before / the previous day**
- this → **that**; these → **those**
- here → **there**
- ago → **before**
- last week → **the previous week**; next week → **the following week**

steps.title: Questions, commands and requests
steps.body:
**Yes/no questions** → *asked if/whether* + statement word order:
*He said to me, “Are you coming?”* → *He asked me **if I was** coming.*

**Wh- questions** → keep the wh-word + statement order (no question mark):
*She asked, “Where do you live?”* → *She asked **where I lived**.*

**Commands** → *told/ordered + (not) to + verb*:
*The teacher said, “Close the door.”* → *The teacher **told us to close** the door.*
*Mother said, “Don't shout.”* → *Mother **told me not to shout**.*

**Requests** → *requested/asked + to*:
*He said, “Please help me.”* → *He **requested me to help** him.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping question order: *She asked where did I live* ✗ → **where I lived**.
- *He said me that…* ✗ → **He told me that…** / **He said to me…** (*tell* takes a person; *say* doesn't need one).
- Forgetting to change pronouns: *Riya said, “I like my school”* → *Riya said that **she** liked **her** school.*
- Adding a question mark to a reported question.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Report these:
1. Kiran said, “I will call you tomorrow.”
2. The doctor said to me, “Drink more water.”
3. Sana asked, “Have you seen my phone?”

*Answers:* 1) Kiran said that she/he would call me the next day. 2) The doctor told me to drink more water. 3) Sana asked if I had seen her phone.

activity.prompt: Complete the reported speech. Direct: Raj said, “I am going to the market today.”
activity.text: Raj said that ___ ___ going to the market ___ ___.

quiz.q: She said, “I like mangoes.” →
options: She told that she liked mangoes.
She said that I liked mangoes.
She said that she liked mangoes.
She said that she likes mangoes.
quiz.why: In indirect speech with a past reporting verb, the tense moves back, 'like' becomes 'liked', and 'I' changes to 'she'. So 'She said that she liked mangoes'.

quiz.q: He asked me, “Where are you going?” →
options: He asked me where are you going?
He said me where I was going.
He asked me where was I going.
He asked me where I was going.
quiz.why: In reported questions, the word order becomes that of a statement, the tense moves back, and there is no question mark. So 'where I was going'.

quiz.q: The teacher said, “Don't run in the corridor.” →
options: The teacher asked that don't run.
The teacher told us to not running.
The teacher told us not to run in the corridor.
The teacher said us don't run.
quiz.why: A negative command is reported with 'told' + object + 'not to' + base verb. So 'told us not to run in the corridor'.

quiz.q: 'tomorrow' in reported speech usually becomes
quiz.why: In reported speech, 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' or 'the following day', since the time is seen from a later point.

quiz.q: He said, “The Sun rises in the east.” →
options: He said that the Sun rose in the east.
He said that the Sun rises in the east.
He said the Sun will rise.
quiz.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense even in reported speech, so 'the Sun rises in the east' does not change.

lessons.title: Punctuation that makes meaning clear

scenes.text: Divya in Mysuru texts her family group: “Lets eat grandma!”
Her cousin Kabir replies with a shocked emoji: “Please don't eat Grandma!”
Divya fixes it: “Let's eat, Grandma!” One comma and one apostrophe saved Grandma. Punctuation isn't decoration — it changes meaning.

steps.title: Capitals and end marks
steps.body:
**Capital letters:** the first word of a sentence; the pronoun **I**; names of people, places, days, months, festivals, languages, nationalities, brands; titles (*Dr Rao*, *The Jungle Book*).

**End marks:**
- **Full stop (.)** — statements and polite commands
- **Question mark (?)** — direct questions only (*Where is he?* — but *I wonder where he is.*)
- **Exclamation mark (!)** — strong feeling; use sparingly, and only one!

steps.title: The comma
steps.body:
Use a **comma (,)**:
- in lists: *I bought rice, dal, oil and salt.* (A comma before 'and' — the Oxford comma — is optional but can prevent confusion.)
- after an introductory word or clause: *However, we left. When the rain stopped, we played.*
- before FANBOYS joining two main clauses: *I called, but nobody answered.*
- around extra information: *My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor.*
- when addressing someone: *Let's eat, Grandma. Ravi, come here.*
- in dates and with direct speech: *On 26 January, 1950, … / She said, “Wait.”*

steps.title: The apostrophe
steps.body:
Two jobs only:
1. **Contractions** — a missing letter: *do not → don't, it is → it's, I am → I'm, they are → they're*
2. **Possession** — belonging:
   - singular: *the girl**'s** bag* (one girl)
   - plural ending in s: *the girls**'** bags* (many girls)
   - plural not ending in s: *the children**'s** books, the men**'s** room*

**Never** use an apostrophe for simple plurals: *mango's for sale* ✗ → **mangoes for sale**.
**its** (belonging) vs **it's** (it is): *The dog wagged **its** tail. **It's** raining.*

steps.title: Quotation marks, colons and more
steps.body:
- **Quotation marks (“ ”)** around exact spoken words. The punctuation of the speech goes **inside**: *“Are you ready?” asked Meena.* Start a new paragraph for each new speaker.
- **Colon (:)** — introduces a list or an explanation: *Bring three things: a pen, a ruler and water.*
- **Semicolon (;)** — joins two closely related main clauses: *It was late; the shops were closed.*
- **Hyphen (-)** — joins words: *a well-known actor, twenty-five, mother-in-law*
- **Dash (—)** — a strong break or aside, used sparingly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *Its a nice day* ✗ → **It's**.
- *Your welcome* ✗ → **You're welcome** (you are).
- *Their going home* ✗ → **They're** (they are); *their* = belonging; *there* = place.
- Comma splice: *I was hungry, I ate* ✗ → *I was hungry, so I ate.*
- Too many exclamation marks!!! ✗

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Punctuate: *where are you going asked rahul im going to the market with my sisters friend said ali*

*Answer:* “Where are you going?” asked Rahul. “I'm going to the market with my sister's friend,” said Ali.

statements.s: ‘The dog chased it's tail.’ is correct.
statements.why: Possessive its has no apostrophe.

statements.s: ‘The children's playground is new.’ is correct.
statements.why: Children is plural without s → children's.

statements.s: ‘I wonder where he is?’ needs a question mark.
statements.why: It's a statement containing an indirect question.

statements.s: ‘They're bringing their books over there.’ is correct.
statements.why: They're = they are; their = belonging; there = place.

statements.s: ‘Tomato's for sale’ correctly uses an apostrophe.
statements.why: Plurals don't take apostrophes: tomatoes.

quiz.q: Which is correctly punctuated?
quiz.why: 'Let's' is the short form of 'let us', and the apostrophe replaces the missing 'u'. So 'Let's go home' is correct.

quiz.q: The ___ uniforms are blue. (many boys)
quiz.why: For a plural noun that already ends in s, add only an apostrophe after the s. So 'the boys' uniforms'.

quiz.q: Where should the comma go? 'After the match we went home.'
options: After the match we, went home.
After the match, we went home.
quiz.why: A comma follows an introductory phrase like 'After the match', and separates it from the main clause. So 'After the match, we went home'.

quiz.q: Choose the correct one: '___ raining again.'
quiz.why: 'It's' is the short form of 'it is', and here 'It's raining' fits. 'Its' without an apostrophe shows possession.

quiz.q: A colon is best used to
quiz.why: A colon is used to introduce a list or explanation, as in 'Bring three things: a pen, a book and a ruler'.

sources: Standard English punctuation (topic reference)

questions.q: A sentence must have a subject and a
questions.why: A sentence needs a subject and a predicate, which contains a verb. Without a verb it is only a phrase.

questions.q: Which is correct?
questions.why: 'It's' means 'it is', and 'It's my book' is correct. 'Its my book' misses the apostrophe, and 'Its'' is never correct.

questions.q: Passive voice uses be +
questions.why: The passive voice is formed with a form of 'be' plus the past participle, such as 'was written'.

questions.q: 'I was tired, ___ I went to bed early.'
questions.why: Being tired caused her to go to bed early, so the second clause is a result. The conjunction for a result is 'so'.

questions.q: Passive of 'Priya cleans the room':
options: The room was cleaned by Priya.
The room is cleaned by Priya.
questions.why: The active simple present 'cleans' becomes 'is cleaned' in the passive. The room is the subject, and 'by Priya' shows the doer.

questions.q: He said, “I am happy.” → He said that he ___ happy.
questions.why: With the reporting verb 'said', 'am' moves back to 'was', and 'I' changes to 'he'. So 'He said that he was happy'.

questions.q: Which is a complex sentence?
options: I sang because I was happy.
questions.why: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause. 'I sang' is main, and 'because I was happy' is subordinate.

questions.q: She asked me, “Did you finish?” →
options: She asked me did I finish.
She asked me if I had finished.
She asked me if I finish?
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', and the tense moves back: 'did you finish' becomes 'I had finished'. There is no question mark.

questions.q: The ___ toys are scattered. (many children)
questions.why: 'Children' is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so we add 's to show possession: 'children's toys'.

questions.q: Passive of 'They have completed the project':
options: The project is completed by them being.
questions.why: The present perfect 'have completed' becomes 'has been completed' in the passive. The project is now the subject.

questions.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
options: Because it was cold, I wore a jacket.
It was cold, so I wore a jacket.
It was cold; I wore a jacket.
It was cold, I wore a jacket.
questions.why: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. 'It was cold, I wore a jacket' needs a conjunction, semicolon or full stop.

questions.q: The coach said, “Practise every day.” →
options: The coach asked practise every day?
The coach told us to practise every day.
The coach told that practise daily.
questions.why: A command is reported with 'told' + object + 'to' + base verb. So 'told us to practise every day'.

questions.q: 'If I ___ the Prime Minister, I would ban plastic bags.'
questions.why: A second conditional about an unreal present uses the past form, and 'were' is used for all persons in standard English. So 'If I were the Prime Minister'.

questions.q: He said, “I met her yesterday.” →
options: He said that he had met her the previous day.
He said that he met her yesterday.
He said he meets her tomorrow.
He said that I had met her today.
questions.why: In reported speech the past tense 'met' becomes the past perfect 'had met', and 'yesterday' changes to 'the previous day'. 'I' changes to 'he'.

courses.title: Writing Well: paragraphs, letters, emails, notices, stories and essays
courses.summary: The practical writing every school and workplace needs: strong paragraphs, formal and informal letters, emails, notices and messages, diary entries, stories and essays — with formats, model answers and a proofreading checklist.
outcomes: Learners can write a paragraph with a topic sentence, supporting details and a conclusion
Learners can write formal and informal letters and emails in the correct format and tone
Learners can write notices, messages and diary entries within word limits
Learners can plan and write narrative and descriptive stories and short essays
Learners can proofread and improve their own writing

lessons.title: The perfect paragraph

scenes.text: In Surat, Aarav writes a paragraph on 'My Pet'. It starts with his dog Bruno, wanders to cricket, then his cousin's wedding, then back to Bruno.
His teacher Ms Kapoor draws a hamburger: top bun (topic sentence), fillings (details), bottom bun (conclusion).
Aarav rewrites it: one main idea, three vivid details about Bruno, and a warm closing line. It's half the length and twice as good.

steps.title: The hamburger structure
steps.body:
A **paragraph** is a group of sentences about **one main idea**.
1. **Topic sentence** — states the main idea. *My dog Bruno is the most loyal friend I have.*
2. **Supporting sentences** (3–5) — details, examples, reasons, facts. *He waits at the gate every afternoon…*
3. **Concluding sentence** — wraps up or links to the next idea. *With Bruno around, I never feel alone.*

Keep it **unified** (everything relates to the topic) and **coherent** (ideas flow logically).

steps.title: Linking words (connectors)
steps.body:
Connectors guide the reader:
- **Adding:** also, moreover, furthermore, in addition
- **Contrast:** however, but, on the other hand, although
- **Cause/effect:** because, therefore, as a result, so
- **Sequence:** first, next, then, after that, finally
- **Example:** for example, for instance, such as
- **Concluding:** in short, overall, in conclusion

steps.title: Model paragraph (about 100 words)
steps.body:
**Topic: Why every school needs a library**

A library is the quiet heart of a good school. **First,** it gives every student — rich or poor — free access to thousands of books. **For example,** a child who cannot buy an encyclopaedia can still explore space, history and science. **Moreover,** reading for pleasure builds vocabulary and imagination far better than any worksheet. A library is **also** a calm place to study, away from noise at home. **In short,** a school without a library is like a garden without water: it may survive, but it will never truly bloom.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No clear topic sentence — the reader doesn't know the point.
- Mixing several unrelated ideas in one paragraph.
- Repeating the same idea in different words to fill space.
- Starting every sentence the same way (*I… I… I…*). Vary your openings.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a paragraph of 80–100 words on **'The best day of my holidays'**. Underline your topic sentence, circle your connectors, and check the last line wraps it up.

activity.prompt: Put these sentences in order to form a good paragraph.
items: Regular exercise has many benefits for teenagers.
First, it strengthens the heart, muscles and bones.
In addition, it helps you sleep better and concentrate in class.
Exercise also reduces stress and lifts your mood.
In short, just 60 minutes of activity a day can make you healthier and happier.

quiz.q: The topic sentence of a paragraph
quiz.why: The topic sentence states the main idea, so the reader knows what the paragraph is about. The rest of the paragraph supports it.

quiz.q: Which connector shows contrast?
quiz.why: 'However' introduces an opposite idea, so it shows contrast. 'Moreover' adds, 'therefore' shows result and 'for example' gives an example.

quiz.q: A paragraph should usually focus on
quiz.why: A good paragraph has unity: it focuses on one main idea. Many ideas make it confusing.

quiz.q: 'As a result' shows
quiz.why: 'As a result' introduces a consequence of what was said before, so it shows cause and effect.

lessons.title: Letters and emails: formal and informal

scenes.text: Ritika in Jaipur needs leave for her sister's wedding. She also wants to tell her best friend Emma in Bristol about the wedding.
Her first draft to the principal starts: “Hey ma'am!! Need 3 days off for my sis's wedding lol.”
Her mother laughs and helps her write two very different letters — one formal, one friendly. Same news, two tones. Ritika gets the leave AND a delighted reply from Emma.

steps.title: Formal letter format
steps.body:
Used for principals, officials, editors, companies, job applications, complaints.

1. **Sender's address** (top left) and **date**
2. **Receiver's designation and address**: *The Principal, ABC School, Jaipur*
3. **Subject line**: *Subject: Application for three days' leave*
4. **Salutation**: *Respected Sir/Madam,* or *Dear Sir/Madam,*
5. **Body** — paragraph 1: purpose; paragraph 2: details; paragraph 3: request/closing
6. **Complimentary close**: *Yours sincerely,* (or *Yours faithfully,* when you start with Sir/Madam, in British usage) / *Yours obediently,* in school leave letters
7. **Name** (and class/roll number or signature)

**Tone:** polite, clear, no slang, no contractions (*do not*, not *don't*).

steps.title: Model: leave application
steps.body:
The Principal
Sunrise Public School
Jaipur

25 November 2026

**Subject: Application for leave from 1 to 3 December**

Respected Madam,

I am Ritika Sharma of Class 7-B. I respectfully request leave for three days, from 1 to 3 December 2026, as I have to attend my elder sister's wedding in Ajmer.

I will complete all the class work and homework I miss after I return.

Kindly grant me leave for these days.

Thank you.

Yours obediently,
Ritika Sharma
Class 7-B, Roll No. 24

steps.title: Informal letters
steps.body:
Used for family and friends. Format:
1. Your address and date
2. **Salutation**: *Dear Emma,* / *Dear Nani,*
3. **Body**: warm opening (*I hope you're doing well*), the news in detail with feelings, questions to the reader, closing wishes
4. **Close**: *With love, / Your friend, / Lots of love,*
5. Your name

**Tone:** friendly and personal — contractions and exclamations are fine, but keep it respectful and clear. No subject line.

steps.title: Emails
steps.body:
- **To:** correct address · **Subject:** short and specific (*Request: extension for science project*)
- **Greeting:** *Dear Mr Khan,* (formal) / *Hi Leo,* (informal)
- **Body:** short paragraphs; the most important point first
- **Close:** *Regards, / Best wishes, / Thank you,* + your name (and class or role)

**Etiquette:** check spelling before sending; no ALL CAPS (it reads as shouting); attach files and mention them; reply within a reasonable time; never share passwords; think before you forward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Slang or text-speak in formal letters (*pls, u, thx, lol*).
- Missing subject line in a formal letter or email.
- Mixing tones — starting *Respected Sir* and ending *Bye!!*
- Too long: get to the point in the first paragraph.
- *Yours Sincerely* (capital S) ✗ → **Yours sincerely** (only the first word capitalised).

a.text: Your science project is due tomorrow, but you have a fever. You need to email your teacher, Mrs Iyer. Which subject line do you choose?

choices.label: “hi”
choices.feedback: Too vague — she won't know what it's about.

choices.label: “Request for extension: Science project (Class 8-A)”
choices.feedback: Clear and specific.

b.text: Mrs Iyer gets 50 emails a day. Want to improve the subject line?

choices.label: Yes — “Request for extension: Science project (Class 8-A)”
choices.feedback: Much better.

choices.label: No, “URGENT!!! READ NOW” is better
choices.feedback: Capitals and exclamation marks look rude.

c.text: Now the body. Which opening works best?

choices.label: “Dear Mrs Iyer, I am unwell with a fever and request a two-day extension for my science project. I have finished most of it and can submit it on Friday.”
choices.feedback: Polite, clear, specific — and offers a solution.

choices.label: “hey mam i cant do project sry”
choices.feedback: Too casual and unclear.

end1.text: Mrs Iyer replies: “Get well soon — Friday is fine.” A clear subject, polite greeting, reason, specific request and a proposed solution work every time.

end2.text: Tip: formal emails need a specific subject, a polite greeting (Dear …), a clear reason and request, and a proper close (Regards, + your name and class).

quiz.q: Which salutation suits a letter to a newspaper editor?
quiz.why: A letter to a newspaper editor is formal, so it uses a formal salutation like 'Dear Sir/Madam'. 'Hey' and 'Hi buddy' are informal.

quiz.q: A subject line is required in
quiz.why: A formal letter or email needs a subject line, which states its purpose briefly. Informal letters, diary entries and poems do not.

quiz.q: Which is the correct closing for a formal letter?
quiz.why: In a formal close, only the first word is capitalised: 'Yours sincerely,'. 'Bye!' is too casual.

quiz.q: In a formal email, writing in ALL CAPITALS
quiz.why: Writing in ALL CAPITALS in an email reads like shouting and seems rude, so it should be avoided.

lessons.title: Notices, messages and diary entries

scenes.text: Shabnam, head girl at a school in Lucknow, must put up a notice about the inter-house quiz on the school board.
The same day she takes a phone call for the sports teacher, who is out, and writes a short message for him.
At night she writes in her diary about how nervous and proud she felt. Three formats, three purposes — and all of them short and clear.

steps.title: Notice
steps.body:
A **notice** informs a group about an event, announcement or instruction. Usually **50 words** in school exams, inside a **box**.

Format:
1. **Name of the institution** (top)
2. **NOTICE** (centred)
3. **Date**
4. **Heading** (in capitals): *INTER-HOUSE QUIZ COMPETITION*
5. **Body** — answer **what, when, where, who (eligible), how (to register), whom to contact**
6. **Name and designation** of the writer (*Shabnam Ali, Head Girl*)

Use the **passive voice** and third person where natural: *All students are informed that…*

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
**CITY MODEL SCHOOL, LUCKNOW**
**NOTICE**
25 November 2026
**INTER-HOUSE QUIZ COMPETITION**

All students of Classes 6–8 are informed that an Inter-House Quiz will be held on 5 December 2026 at 10 a.m. in the school auditorium. Each house may send a team of three. Interested students should give their names to their House Captains by 1 December.

Shabnam Ali
Head Girl

steps.title: Message
steps.body:
A **message** passes on information to someone who wasn't there (phone call, visitor). About **50 words**, in a box.

Format: **MESSAGE** · date and **time** · *Dear …* · the message (who called, what they said, what to do) · your name

Use **reported speech**: *Mr Sinha called. He said the match had been shifted to Friday and asked you to call him back by 6 p.m.*

steps.title: Diary entry
steps.body:
A **diary entry** is personal writing about your experiences, thoughts and feelings.

Format: **Day, date (and time)** at the top · *Dear Diary,* (optional) · body · your name (optional)

Style: **first person**, **past tense** for events, present for current feelings; informal and honest. Include **what happened, how you felt, what you learned**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the box, date, heading or designation in a notice.
- Writing a notice like a letter (*Dear students…*) — notices don't have salutations.
- Messages that leave out the time or what action is needed.
- Exceeding the word limit — in exams, examiners may deduct marks.

activity.prompt: Before you put up a notice, check you have included:
items: Name of the institution
The word NOTICE
Date
A heading in capital letters
What the event is
Date, time and venue of the event
Who is eligible / who should act
How and by when to register or respond
Writer's name and designation
About 50 words, inside a box

quiz.q: A notice usually has
options: a heading, date and writer's designation
quiz.why: A notice is an announcement, so it has a heading, date and the writer's designation. It does not have a salutation or a complimentary close like a letter.

quiz.q: A message should always include
options: the time and what action is needed
quiz.why: A message must tell the reader the time and what action is needed, so they know when and what to do.

quiz.q: Diary entries are usually written in the
quiz.why: Diary entries are personal, so they are written in the first person ('I').

quiz.q: Typical length for a school-exam notice is about
quiz.why: A notice in a school exam is usually about 50 words, since it must be short and complete.

lessons.title: Stories, descriptions and essays

scenes.text: Kofi, a Ghanaian student in Bengaluru, and his classmate Priya enter a story contest on the theme 'The Storm'.
Priya's first draft: “There was a storm. It was very bad. Then it stopped.” Kofi's: “The sky turned the colour of a bruise, and the first fat raindrops drummed on the tin roof.”
Priya laughs and asks how he did it. 'Show, don't tell,' Kofi says. 'Use your five senses.' Her second draft makes the judges shiver.

steps.title: Story structure
steps.body:
Most good stories follow this arc:
1. **Beginning** — introduce the **characters** and **setting** (where, when); hook the reader
2. **Problem/conflict** — something goes wrong or a challenge appears
3. **Rising action** — attempts, tension grows
4. **Climax** — the most exciting or important moment
5. **Resolution** — how it ends; what changed or was learned

Give your story a **title**, use **past tense** consistently, and include some **dialogue** (with correct punctuation).

steps.title: Show, don't tell
steps.body:
**Tell:** *She was nervous.*
**Show:** *Her hands were damp, and she read the first line of her speech three times without seeing it.*

Use the **five senses**: sight, sound, smell, touch, taste.
Use **strong verbs** (*stormed, whispered, staggered*) instead of weak verb + adverb (*walked angrily*).
Use **figurative language**: **simile** (*as quiet as a library*, *like a frightened cat*), **metaphor** (*the classroom was a zoo*), **personification** (*the wind howled*).

steps.title: Essays
steps.body:
An essay presents ideas on a topic in organised paragraphs.

**Types:** **descriptive** (a place, person, event), **narrative** (a personal experience), **argumentative/discursive** (*Should mobile phones be allowed in school?*), **expository** (explaining: *The importance of trees*).

**Structure:**
- **Introduction** — hook (a question, fact or short anecdote) + your main idea
- **Body** — 2–4 paragraphs, one point each, with examples
- **Conclusion** — sum up and end with a thought, suggestion or call to action

**Plan first (2–3 minutes):** jot down 3 main points and an example for each. Planning saves time and prevents wandering.

steps.title: Common mistakes and proofreading
steps.body:
- Switching tense halfway through a story.
- Endings like *and then I woke up — it was a dream* (often feels like a cheat).
- Copying memorised essays — examiners notice; your own examples score better.
- No paragraphs — a wall of text is hard to read.

**Proofread** with **COPS**: **C**apitals, **O**rganisation, **P**unctuation, **S**pelling. Read aloud quietly — your ear catches errors your eye misses.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Rewrite these 'tell' sentences as 'show' sentences:
1. The market was crowded.
2. He was very angry.
3. The food was delicious.

Then write a 150-word story beginning: *The power went off just as…*

activity.prompt: Match the literary device to its example.
pairs: Her voice was as sweet as honey.
The wind whispered through the trees.

quiz.q: The most exciting moment of a story is the
quiz.why: The climax is the most exciting moment of a story, where tension is highest. The introduction and setting come earlier.

quiz.q: 'The sun smiled down on us' is an example of
quiz.why: Giving the sun a human action, smiling, is personification. A simile uses 'like' or 'as', and hyperbole is exaggeration.

quiz.q: 'Show, don't tell' means
options: use details and actions so the reader feels the emotion
quiz.why: 'Show, don't tell' means using details and actions so that the reader feels the emotion, rather than just naming it.

quiz.q: An argumentative essay
options: presents a view on an issue with reasons
quiz.why: An argumentative essay presents a view on an issue and supports it with reasons and evidence. It is not just a description.

quiz.q: COPS proofreading stands for
quiz.why: COPS is a proofreading checklist: Capitals, Organisation, Punctuation and Spelling.

lessons.title: Integers: numbers below zero

scenes.text: At 6 a.m. in Leh, Tenzin's thermometer reads −8 °C. By 2 p.m. it shows +5 °C. 'How much warmer is it?' asks his little sister Dolma.
Dolma guesses 3 degrees, because 8 − 5 = 3. Tenzin draws a number line on the frosty window to check.
From −8 up to 0 is 8 steps; from 0 up to +5 is 5 more steps. Total 13 degrees warmer! Negative numbers are real — in temperatures, bank overdrafts, floors below ground and sea depths.

steps.title: What integers are
steps.body:
**Integers** are the whole numbers together with their negatives: … −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 …

- Positive integers lie to the **right** of 0 on the number line.
- Negative integers lie to the **left** of 0.
- 0 is neither positive nor negative.

Every integer has an **opposite** (additive inverse): the opposite of 7 is −7, and 7 + (−7) = 0.

**Comparing:** a number further right is always greater. So −2 > −9 (−2 is closer to zero, further right), even though 9 looks bigger.

steps.title: Adding integers
steps.body:
**Rule 1 — same signs:** add the sizes, keep the sign.
- (+6) + (+4) = +10
- (−6) + (−4) = −10 (owing ₹6 and then owing ₹4 means owing ₹10)

**Rule 2 — different signs:** subtract the smaller size from the bigger size, keep the sign of the bigger size.
- (−9) + 5 = −4 (9 − 5 = 4, and 9 was negative)
- 12 + (−7) = +5

**On the number line:** start at the first number; adding a positive moves right, adding a negative moves left.

steps.title: Subtracting = adding the opposite
steps.body:
To subtract an integer, **add its opposite**.

- 5 − 8 = 5 + (−8) = −3
- 5 − (−8) = 5 + 8 = 13
- −4 − (−10) = −4 + 10 = 6

Tenzin's question: 5 − (−8) = 13 degrees warmer. ✔️

Why does 'minus a minus' become plus? Taking away a debt makes you richer. If someone cancels your ₹8 debt, your money goes up by ₹8.

steps.title: Multiplying and dividing integers
steps.body:
Multiply or divide the sizes, then fix the sign:

- same signs → **positive**: (−3) × (−4) = 12, (−20) ÷ (−5) = 4
- different signs → **negative**: (−3) × 4 = −12, 20 ÷ (−5) = −4

With many factors, **count the negative signs**: an even number of them gives a positive answer, an odd number gives a negative one.
(−1) × (−2) × (−3) = −6 (three negatives → negative).

Anything × 0 = 0. Division by 0 is **not defined**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking −9 > −2 because 9 > 2. On the number line −9 is further left, so it is **smaller**.
- Using the multiplication rule for addition: (−3) + (−4) is −7, not +7.
- Forgetting brackets: −3² means −(3×3) = −9, but (−3)² = 9.
- Writing 5 − (−2) = 3. It is 5 + 2 = 7.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. A submarine is at −120 m. It rises 45 m. Where is it now?
2. Work out (−15) ÷ 3 × (−2).
3. Put in order, smallest first: 4, −7, 0, −1, −12.

*Answers:* 1) −75 m 2) −5 × (−2) = 10 3) −12, −7, −1, 0, 4

activity.prompt: Mumbai's cold-storage room is at −18 °C. The power fails and the temperature rises by 25 °C. What is the new temperature (in °C)?

quiz.q: Which is greater: −3 or −11?
quiz.why: On the number line, −3 is to the right of −11, so −3 is greater. With negatives, the number closer to zero is larger.
Both numbers are negative, so add their sizes, 7 + 6 = 13, and keep the negative sign, giving −13.
Subtracting −5 is the same as adding +5, so 8 − (−5) = 8 + 5 = 13.
Three negative signs give a negative product. 4 × 5 × 1 = 20, so the answer is −20.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
quiz.why: Opposites add to zero: −6 + 6 = 0. 0 is neither positive nor negative, and division by zero is undefined.

lessons.title: Fractions: parts of a whole, done properly

scenes.text: Amara ordered two pizzas for her study group in Lagos. One was cut into 8 slices, the other into 6.
Kunle ate 3 slices of the first (3/8) and 2 of the second (2/6). 'So I ate 5/14 of a pizza,' he said. Amara laughed — that can't be right.
Slices of different sizes can't be added directly. They made the slices the same size first: 3/8 + 1/3 = 9/24 + 8/24 = 17/24 of a pizza.

steps.title: What a fraction means
steps.body:
A fraction **a/b** means: split one whole into **b equal parts** (the **denominator**) and take **a** of them (the **numerator**).

- **Proper** fraction: numerator < denominator, e.g. 3/5 (less than 1).
- **Improper** fraction: numerator ≥ denominator, e.g. 7/4.
- **Mixed number:** 7/4 = 1¾ (7 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 3).

**Equivalent fractions** name the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the **same** non-zero number.

**Simplest form:** divide top and bottom by their HCF. 18/24 → HCF 6 → 3/4.

steps.title: Comparing fractions
steps.body:
Same denominator: compare numerators (5/9 > 2/9).

Different denominators: make them the same using the **LCM**.
Compare 5/6 and 7/9. LCM(6, 9) = 18.
- 5/6 = 15/18
- 7/9 = 14/18
So 5/6 > 7/9.

Shortcut (cross-multiplying): 5 × 9 = 45 and 7 × 6 = 42; 45 > 42 so 5/6 is bigger.

steps.title: Adding and subtracting
steps.body:
**Only add numerators when denominators are equal.**

2/3 + 1/4: LCM(3, 4) = 12 → 8/12 + 3/12 = **11/12**

3½ − 1⅔: convert to improper fractions: 7/2 − 5/3 = 21/6 − 10/6 = 11/6 = **1⅚**

Kunle's mistake (3/8 + 2/6 = 5/14) adds bottoms too. Denominators tell you the **size** of the pieces — they are never added.

steps.title: Multiplying and dividing
steps.body:
**Multiply:** top × top, bottom × bottom. 2/3 × 9/10 = 18/30 = 3/5. (Cancel first to keep numbers small: 2/3 × 9/10 → 1/1 × 3/5.)

'**of**' means multiply: 3/4 of 60 = 3/4 × 60 = 45.

**Divide:** multiply by the **reciprocal** (flip the second fraction).
3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8/1 = 6. Check: how many eighths fit into three quarters? 6 of them.

Mixed numbers must be made improper before multiplying or dividing: 1½ × 2⅓ = 3/2 × 7/3 = 7/2 = 3½.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 ≠ 2/5. (It is 5/6.)
- Flipping the **first** fraction when dividing. Flip only the divisor (the second one).
- Multiplying mixed numbers part by part: 1½ × 2⅓ is not 2 + 1/6.
- Forgetting to simplify the final answer.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Riya walks 3/4 km to school and 2/5 km to tuition. Total?
2. A 2½ m ribbon is cut into pieces of 1/4 m. How many pieces?
3. Which is bigger, 4/7 or 5/9?

*Answers:* 1) 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20 km 2) 5/2 ÷ 1/4 = 10 pieces 3) 4×9 = 36 > 5×7 = 35, so 4/7

activity.prompt: Match each calculation to its answer.

quiz.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 3/5?
quiz.why: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 3/5 by 3 to get 9/15. Equivalent fractions have the same value.
The LCM of 4 and 3 is 12, so 1/4 = 3/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. Adding gives 11/12.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: 5/6 × 12/5 = 60/30 = 2.

quiz.q: What is 2/3 of 45?
quiz.why: Find 1/3 of 45 first: 45 ÷ 3 = 15. Then 2/3 is 15 × 2 = 30.

quiz.q: Write 23/5 as a mixed number.
quiz.why: 23 ÷ 5 gives 4 with remainder 3, so 23/5 = 4 3/5. The whole number is the quotient and the remainder goes over 5.

lessons.title: Decimals: place value after the point

story.title: Grace and the cricket bat price

scenes.text: Grace in Kochi wants a bat costing ₹1,249.50 and gloves costing ₹375.75. She has ₹1,600.
Her friend Sanju lines the numbers up wrongly and gets a silly answer. Grace lines up the decimal points: 1249.50 + 375.75 = 1625.25.
She is ₹25.25 short. She decides to buy the gloves next month. Decimals are just fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 — and the point keeps everything in its place.

steps.title: Place value
steps.body:
In **345.678**:
- 3 hundreds, 4 tens, 5 ones
- 6 **tenths** (6/10), 7 **hundredths** (7/100), 8 **thousandths** (8/1000)

So 0.7 = 7/10, 0.07 = 7/100, 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4.

Adding zeros at the **end** after the point changes nothing: 2.5 = 2.50 = 2.500. That helps when comparing: 0.6 vs 0.58 → 0.60 vs 0.58 → 0.6 is bigger.

steps.title: Fractions ↔ decimals
steps.body:
**Fraction → decimal:** divide top by bottom.
- 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
- 1/3 = 0.333… (a **recurring** decimal)

**Decimal → fraction:** write over 10, 100, 1000 and simplify.
- 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20
- 2.125 = 2125/1000 = 17/8

Useful ones to remember: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/8 = 0.125.

steps.title: Calculating with decimals
steps.body:
**Add/subtract:** line up the decimal points. 12.4 − 3.75 → 12.40 − 3.75 = 8.65

**Multiply:** ignore the points, multiply, then count the total decimal places in the question.
2.4 × 0.3 → 24 × 3 = 72; places 1 + 1 = 2 → **0.72**

**× and ÷ by 10, 100, 1000:** move the point right (×) or left (÷) by the number of zeros.
3.6 × 100 = 360; 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452

**Divide by a decimal:** make the divisor whole. 4.8 ÷ 0.6 = 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Longer means bigger': 0.125 is **less** than 0.5.
- Lining up the right-hand digits instead of the points when adding.
- 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.9 ✗ — it is 0.09 (two decimal places).
- Thinking multiplying always makes things bigger: 50 × 0.2 = 10.

steps.title: Decimals around you
steps.body:
- Money: ₹45.50 means 45 rupees 50 paise.
- Measurement: 1.75 m = 1 m 75 cm; 2.5 kg = 2 kg 500 g.
- Sports: a 100 m sprint time of 10.85 s; batting averages like 48.37.
- Petrol bills, electricity units, body temperature (37.2 °C).

activity.prompt: Sort each number: is it less than one half, or more than one half?

quiz.q: What is the place value of 4 in 23.548?
quiz.why: After the decimal point the places are tenths (5), hundredths (4) and thousandths (8). So the 4 stands for 4 hundredths.
Multiply 6 × 4 = 24 ignoring the points. There is one decimal place in each number, so the answer has 2 decimal places: 0.24.

quiz.q: Which is the largest?
quiz.why: Write them with 3 decimal places: 0.900, 0.890, 0.099, 0.090. The largest is 0.900, which is 0.9.

quiz.q: 0.35 as a fraction in simplest form is
quiz.why: 0.35 = 35/100. Divide top and bottom by 5 to simplify to 7/20.
Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the left. 56.3 becomes 0.563.

sources: NCERT Mathematics Class 6–7 (Decimals) — topic reference

lessons.title: Exponents and powers: shorthand for huge and tiny

scenes.text: Ishaan in Pune forwards a fake 'school holiday' message to 2 friends. Each of them forwards it to 2 more, and so on.
After 1 round: 2 people. After 2 rounds: 4. After 10 rounds: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 people. After 20 rounds: over a million!
His teacher Mrs Fernandes shows the class why powers grow so fast — and why checking before forwarding matters. Exponents are the maths of fast growth.

steps.title: Base and exponent
steps.body:
**aⁿ** means a multiplied by itself n times.
- a is the **base**, n is the **exponent** (or power, or index).
- 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32
- 10³ = 1000
- (−3)² = 9 but (−3)³ = −27 (negative base: even power → positive, odd power → negative)

**Watch out:** 2⁵ is NOT 2 × 5.

steps.title: The laws of exponents
steps.body:
For non-zero a, b and integers m, n:
- **aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ** → 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁶
- **aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ** → 5⁷ ÷ 5³ = 5⁴
- **(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ** → (2³)² = 2⁶
- **aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ** → 2³ × 5³ = 10³
- **a⁰ = 1** → 7⁰ = 1 (because 7³ ÷ 7³ = 7⁰ and also = 1)
- **a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ** → 2⁻³ = 1/8 (Class 8)

The laws only work when the **bases are the same** (or the powers are the same, for the 4th law).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. Simplify (2⁵ × 2³) ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = **16**
2. Simplify (3²)³ × 3⁻⁴ = 3⁶ × 3⁻⁴ = 3² = **9**
3. Find x if 5ˣ = 125: 125 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³, so **x = 3**
4. Express 432 as a product of prime powers: 432 = 16 × 27 = **2⁴ × 3³**

steps.title: Standard form (scientific notation)
steps.body:
Write a number as **k × 10ⁿ** where 1 ≤ k < 10.

- Distance from Earth to Sun ≈ 150,000,000 km = **1.5 × 10⁸ km**
- Speed of light ≈ 300,000 km/s = **3 × 10⁵ km/s**
- Small numbers (Class 8): 0.000 007 m = **7 × 10⁻⁶ m**

Count how many places the decimal point moves: left → positive power, right → negative power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 3⁴ × 3² = 9⁶ ✗ — keep the base: 3⁶.
- 2³ + 2² = 2⁵ ✗ — laws are for × and ÷, not + (8 + 4 = 12, not 32).
- 5⁰ = 0 ✗ — it is 1.
- 45 × 10⁴ is not in standard form (45 is not below 10). Correct: 4.5 × 10⁵.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Simplify 7⁹ ÷ 7⁷.
2. Write 6,400,000 in standard form.
3. Evaluate (−2)⁵.
4. Find x: 2ˣ × 2³ = 2¹⁰.

*Answers:* 1) 7² = 49 2) 6.4 × 10⁶ 3) −32 4) x = 7

statements.why: Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1.
Same base: add exponents, 3 + 2 = 5.
An odd power of a negative number is negative: −1.

statements.s: 23 × 10⁵ is in standard form
statements.why: k must be at least 1 and less than 10: 2.3 × 10⁶.

quiz.q: Simplify 6⁵ ÷ 6².
quiz.why: When dividing powers of the same base, subtract the exponents: 6⁵ ÷ 6² = 6⁵⁻² = 6³.
For a power of a power, multiply the exponents: (5²)³ = 5²ˣ³ = 5⁶. Adding gives 5⁵, which is wrong.

quiz.q: Standard form of 0.00042 is
quiz.why: Move the decimal point 4 places to the right to get 4.2, so the power of 10 is −4. In standard form the first number is between 1 and 10.

quiz.q: If 3ˣ = 81, then x = ?
quiz.why: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81, so 3⁴ = 81 and x = 4. 3³ is 27, which is too small.

quiz.q: Which is equal to 1?
options: Any non-zero number to the power 0
quiz.why: Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1, so the full statement is the general rule, not just 1⁰. 0¹ is 0 and 10¹ is 10.

sources: NCERT Mathematics Class 7–8 (Exponents and Powers) — topic reference

questions.q: Which integer is the smallest?
questions.why: On the number line, the further left a number is, the smaller it is. −15 is furthest left, so it is the smallest.
The signs differ, so subtract the sizes: 20 − 12 = 8, and take the sign of the larger size, which is positive. So the answer is 8.

questions.q: Which decimal equals 3/4?
questions.why: 3/4 = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. You can also write it as 75/100.
The signs differ, so the product is negative. 6 × 7 = 42, so the answer is −42.
The LCM of 5 and 2 is 10, so 2/5 = 4/10 and 1/2 = 5/10. Their sum is 9/10.
Multiply 12 × 5 = 60. There are 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places in total, so the answer is 0.060, or 0.06.

questions.q: At midnight in Shimla it was −4 °C; at noon it was 9 °C. The rise was
questions.why: The rise = final − initial = 9 − (−4) = 9 + 4 = 13 °C. Subtracting a negative number means adding.

questions.q: How many 3/8 kg packets can be filled from 6 kg of rice?
questions.why: Number of packets = 6 ÷ 3/8 = 6 × 8/3 = 48/3 = 16. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

questions.q: Simplify (2³ × 2⁴) ÷ 2⁵.
questions.why: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ by adding the powers, and 2⁷ ÷ 2⁵ = 2² = 4 by subtracting them.
There are four negative numbers, an even count, so the product is positive. 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

questions.q: Which is the standard form of 72,500,000?
questions.why: Standard form needs a number between 1 and 10 times a power of 10. 72,500,000 = 7.25 × 10,000,000 = 7.25 × 10⁷.

questions.q: Arrange 5/8, 0.6, 2/3 from smallest to largest.
questions.why: As decimals, 0.6 = 0.600, 5/8 = 0.625 and 2/3 = 0.666…, so the order from smallest to largest is 0.6, 5/8, 2/3.

questions.q: Find x if (3²)ˣ = 3⁸.
questions.why: (3²)ˣ = 3²ˣ, so 3²ˣ = 3⁸ means 2x = 8. Therefore x = 4.

lessons.title: Ratios: comparing by division

scenes.text: In Mysuru, Kavya's Nani makes dosa batter with 3 cups of rice for every 1 cup of urad dal.
Kavya wants to make a big batch for her school fair with 12 cups of rice. How much dal does she need?
Rice : dal = 3 : 1 = 12 : 4. She needs 4 cups of dal. Keeping the ratio the same keeps the taste the same!

steps.title: What a ratio is
steps.body:
A **ratio** compares two quantities **of the same kind, in the same units**, by division.

Ratio of a to b is written **a : b** (read 'a is to b') and equals a/b.

- 3 boys and 5 girls: boys : girls = 3 : 5.
- Order matters: girls : boys = 5 : 3 — a different ratio.
- A ratio has **no unit**.

steps.title: Simplifying and same units
steps.body:
Divide both terms by their HCF.
- 24 : 36 → HCF 12 → **2 : 3**

Convert to the same unit first:
- 50 paise : ₹2 → 50 paise : 200 paise → **1 : 4**
- 45 minutes : 1.5 hours → 45 : 90 → **1 : 2**

**Equivalent ratios:** 2 : 3 = 4 : 6 = 20 : 30 (multiply both terms by the same number).

steps.title: Dividing an amount in a ratio
steps.body:
Share ₹600 between Arjun and Bela in the ratio 2 : 3.

1. Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5
2. One part = 600 ÷ 5 = ₹120
3. Arjun = 2 × 120 = **₹240**, Bela = 3 × 120 = **₹360**

Check: 240 + 360 = 600 ✔ and 240 : 360 = 2 : 3 ✔

steps.title: Proportion
steps.body:
Four numbers are **in proportion** if the two ratios are equal: a : b = c : d, written a : b :: c : d.

Test: **product of extremes = product of means** → a × d = b × c.

Is 3 : 4 :: 15 : 20? 3 × 20 = 60, 4 × 15 = 60 → **yes**.

Find x: 5 : 8 = x : 40 → 8x = 200 → **x = 25**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units: 1 m : 25 cm is 100 : 25 = 4 : 1, not 1 : 25.
- Reversing the order the question asks for.
- Dividing ₹600 in 2 : 3 as ₹200 and ₹300 (that only uses 500!). Always add the parts first.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:

2. Divide 84 marbles between Leo and Mia in the ratio 3 : 4.
3. Are 2 : 7 and 6 : 21 in proportion?

*Answers:* 1) 1000 : 250 = 4 : 1 2) 36 and 48 3) Yes (2 × 21 = 7 × 6 = 42)

lessons.title: The unitary method and direct proportion

scenes.text: Rohan's uncle drives an auto-rickshaw in Jaipur. On a steady day's driving he uses 3 kg of CNG for 90 km.
Tomorrow he has a 150 km wedding trip. How much fuel will he need?
Rohan finds the value of ONE unit first: 90 km ÷ 3 = 30 km per kg. So 150 km needs 150 ÷ 30 = 5 kg. That's the unitary method.

steps.title: Find the value of one
steps.body:
**Unitary method:** first find the value of **one unit**, then multiply for the number of units you need.

5 notebooks cost ₹175. Cost of 8?
- 1 notebook = 175 ÷ 5 = ₹35
- 8 notebooks = 35 × 8 = **₹280**

steps.title: Direct proportion
steps.body:
Two quantities are in **direct proportion** if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the **same** number. Their **ratio stays constant**: x/y = k.

Examples: number of items and total cost; distance and fuel used (at steady speed); hours worked and wages.

On a graph, direct proportion gives a **straight line through the origin**.

steps.title: Inverse proportion (Class 8)
steps.body:
Two quantities are in **inverse proportion** if, when one increases, the other decreases so that their **product stays constant**: x × y = k.

Example: 6 workers paint a wall in 4 days (6 × 4 = 24 worker-days). 8 workers take 24 ÷ 8 = **3 days**.

Other examples: speed and time for a fixed distance; number of children sharing a fixed box of sweets and sweets per child.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. A train covers 240 km in 3 hours at steady speed. How far in 5 hours? 1 hour → 80 km; 5 hours → **400 km** (direct).
2. A hostel has food for 60 students for 20 days. If 75 students come, how long will it last? 60 × 20 = 1200 student-days; 1200 ÷ 75 = **16 days** (inverse).
3. A map scale 1 : 50,000 — 4 cm on the map = 200,000 cm = **2 km** on the ground.

steps.title: Ask: more → more, or more → less?
steps.body:
Before calculating, ask: if one quantity goes up, does the other go up (direct) or down (inverse)?

Mistake: '4 taps fill a tank in 6 hours, so 8 taps take 12 hours.' More taps should take **less** time: 4 × 6 = 24 tap-hours ÷ 8 = 3 hours.

Some things are **neither**: a person's age and height are not in proportion.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. 12 bananas cost ₹60. Cost of 20?
2. A car at 60 km/h takes 5 hours. How long at 75 km/h?
3. A photo 4 cm wide and 6 cm tall is enlarged to 10 cm wide. New height?

*Answers:* 1) ₹100 2) 300 ÷ 75 = 4 h 3) 15 cm

lessons.title: Percentages: out of a hundred

scenes.text: Fatima in Hyderabad scored 42 out of 50 in Science and 68 out of 80 in Maths. Her brother asks, 'Which subject did you do better in?'
68 looks bigger than 42, but the totals are different.
She converts both to percentages: Science 42/50 × 100 = 84%; Maths 68/80 × 100 = 85%. Maths, just barely! Percentages let you compare fairly.

steps.title: Three key question types
steps.body:
1. **Find a percentage of an amount:** 15% of ₹800 = 15/100 × 800 = **₹120**
2. **What percentage is A of B?** (A/B) × 100. 18 out of 24 → 18/24 × 100 = **75%**
3. **Find the whole from a part:** 30% of a number is 45 → number = 45 × 100/30 = **150**

steps.title: Percentage increase and decrease
steps.body:
**% change = (change ÷ original) × 100**

A school's students grew from 800 to 920. Increase = 120. % increase = 120/800 × 100 = **15%**.

A phone's price fell from ₹15,000 to ₹12,000. Decrease = 3000. % decrease = 3000/15000 × 100 = **20%**.

**Multiplier shortcut:** increase by 15% → × 1.15; decrease by 20% → × 0.80.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Dividing by the **new** value instead of the original.
- A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall does **not** return to the start: 100 → 110 → 99.
- '50% off, then an extra 20% off' is not 70% off: 100 → 50 → 40, so 60% off overall.
- 'Percentage points' differ from per cent: a rate going from 4% to 6% rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 50% increase.

steps.title: Where you meet percentages
steps.body:
- Exam marks and cut-offs
- GST on bills (different rates apply to different items)
- Battery charge on your phone
- Election results and survey reports
- Nutrition labels: '% of daily value'
