lessons.title: Mirrors, lenses and colours

scenes.text: In Puducherry, Grandma Rosa uses a magnifying glass to read the tiny print on her medicine strips.
Her grandson Arul notices the car's side mirror says 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear'.
After rain, a rainbow appears. Arul discovers all three — the magnifier, the car mirror and the rainbow — are about light bending or bouncing in curved or clear materials.

steps.title: Curved (spherical) mirrors
steps.body:
Look at both sides of a shiny steel spoon:
- **Concave mirror** (curved inward, like the inside of a spoon): can form **real, inverted** images (which can be caught on a screen) when the object is far, and **enlarged, upright** images when the object is very close. **Converges** light.
  Uses: torch and headlight reflectors, shaving/make-up mirrors, dentists' mirrors, solar cookers.
- **Convex mirror** (bulging outward, the back of the spoon): always forms **virtual, erect, smaller** images and shows a **wider view**.
  Uses: rear-view and side mirrors of vehicles, mirrors at blind turns on hill roads.

steps.title: Lenses
steps.body:
A **lens** is a piece of transparent material (glass or plastic) with curved surfaces. Light **bends (refracts)** as it passes through.
- **Convex lens** — thicker in the middle. **Converges** light to a point. Close objects look **enlarged and upright** → **magnifying glass**. Can form real inverted images of distant objects (try focusing the image of a far window on paper).
- **Concave lens** — thinner in the middle. **Diverges** light. Always forms **virtual, erect, smaller** images.

Lenses are used in spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and our own **eye**.

steps.title: White light is a mixture of colours
steps.body:
A **prism** splits white light into a band of seven colours, a **spectrum**: **VIBGYOR** (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). This splitting is called **dispersion**.

A **rainbow** forms when sunlight is dispersed by tiny raindrops; you see it when the Sun is **behind** you.

**Newton's disc:** a disc painted with the seven colours appears nearly white when spun fast — the colours combine.

steps.title: Our eyes (Class 8)
steps.body:
The eye has a convex **lens** that focuses light on the **retina** at the back, which sends signals through the **optic nerve** to the brain. The **iris** (coloured part) controls the size of the **pupil**, letting in more light in the dark.

Care: read in good light, take screen breaks (look at something far away every 20 minutes or so), never rub eyes hard, splash with clean water if dust enters, and see an eye doctor if vision is blurry. Vitamin A is important for vision. **Braille** lets visually impaired people read by touch.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Mixing up concave/convex **mirrors** with concave/convex **lenses** — mirrors reflect, lenses let light through.
- Thinking convex mirrors magnify — they make images **smaller** (that's why objects are 'closer than they appear').
- **Never** focus sunlight with a lens on skin, paper near people, or look at the Sun through any lens — it can burn and blind.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the lens-optics lab, move an object closer to a convex lens. Note when the image is real and inverted and when it becomes virtual, upright and magnified. Then swap to a concave lens. Does its image ever become real?

activity.prompt: Match the optical device to its use.

quiz.q: Which mirror gives a wider field of view?
quiz.why: A convex mirror gives a wider field of view, though its image is smaller. A plane or concave mirror shows less area.

quiz.q: A magnifying glass is a
quiz.why: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, which makes close objects look larger. A concave lens makes them smaller.

quiz.q: VIBGYOR describes
quiz.why: VIBGYOR stands for violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, the colours of the spectrum of white light.

quiz.q: The part of the eye that controls the pupil size is the
quiz.why: The iris is the coloured part of the eye that widens or narrows the pupil, controlling how much light enters.

quiz.q: A concave lens always forms an image that is
quiz.why: A concave lens spreads light rays apart, so it always forms a virtual, erect and smaller image.

lessons.title: Electric circuits and effects of current

story.title: The power cut at Bilal's house

scenes.text: During a power cut in Srinagar, Bilal finds a torch that won't light. He opens it: the cells are in the wrong way round.
He flips one cell, and the bulb glows. Next day, the MCB in the house switches off when his mother runs the heater, the iron and the geyser together.
His sister Nusrat, an electrician-in-training, explains: current needs a complete path, and too much current heats wires — the MCB protects the house from fire.

steps.title: Cells and circuits
steps.body:
An **electric cell** has a **positive (+)** terminal (the metal cap) and a **negative (−)** terminal (the flat base). Two or more cells joined + to − form a **battery**.

A **circuit** is a complete path for current from the + terminal, through the devices, back to the − terminal.
- **Closed circuit:** the path is complete → the bulb glows.
- **Open circuit:** there is a break (switch OFF, loose wire) → no current.

A **switch** simply opens or closes the circuit. A bulb's thin coiled **filament** glows when current passes; if it breaks, the bulb is **fused**.

steps.title: Circuit symbols (Class 7)
steps.body:
Scientists draw circuits with symbols:
- **Cell:** a long thin line (+) and a short thick line (−)
- **Battery:** several cells joined
- **Switch:** a gap with a lever (open) or a joined line (closed)
- **Bulb:** a circle with a cross or loop inside
- **Wire:** a straight line

A **circuit diagram** shows how parts connect, not how they look.

steps.title: Conductors and insulators
steps.body:
- **Conductors** let current pass: metals (copper, aluminium, iron), graphite (pencil lead), our body, tap water (because of dissolved salts).
- **Insulators** don't: plastic, rubber, wood (dry), glass, paper.

Wires are copper inside (conductor) and plastic outside (insulator). Electricians use rubber gloves and tools with plastic handles.

**Chemical effect (Class 8):** some liquids conduct (salty or lemony water) and current can cause chemical changes in them — used in **electroplating** (e.g. a thin chromium or silver coating).

steps.title: Heating and magnetic effects
steps.body:
**Heating effect:** current passing through a wire heats it. Used in electric irons, heaters, kettles, toasters and geysers (heating **element**).

**Safety:** if too much current flows (too many appliances or a **short circuit**), wires overheat. A **fuse** (a wire that melts) or an **MCB** (miniature circuit breaker, which switches off) breaks the circuit to prevent fires. Use ISI-marked appliances.

**Magnetic effect:** a current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet — it deflects a compass needle. A coil wrapped around an iron nail becomes an **electromagnet**, which works only while the current flows. Used in electric bells, cranes for scrap iron, motors and speakers.

steps.title: Electricity safety — read this
steps.body:
- **Never** experiment with the mains supply or wall sockets. Use only cells (torch batteries) for experiments.
- Don't touch switches with wet hands; keep water away from sockets and appliances.
- Don't overload one socket with many plugs; replace damaged wires.
- Never fly kites near power lines or climb electric poles.
- If someone gets an electric shock, **don't touch them** — switch off the mains or push them away using a dry wooden or plastic object, and call **112**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the circuit lab, build a circuit with one cell, a switch and a bulb. Then add a second bulb. Does it get dimmer? Add a second cell. Then test a pencil lead, a plastic ruler, a coin and a rubber band — which ones let the bulb glow?

statements.s: A bulb glows only in a closed circuit.
statements.why: Current needs a complete path.

statements.s: Rubber is a good conductor of electricity.
statements.why: Rubber is an insulator.

statements.s: An MCB switches off the circuit when too much current flows.
statements.why: It protects wires from overheating.

statements.s: An electromagnet stays magnetic after the current is switched off.
statements.why: Its magnetism (mostly) disappears when current stops.

statements.s: It is safe to test wall sockets with a wire if you are careful.
statements.why: Mains electricity can kill. Use only cells for experiments.

statements.s: The heating effect of current is used in an electric iron.
statements.why: Its element heats when current flows.

quiz.q: A circuit with a break in it is
quiz.why: A circuit with a break in it is open, so no current flows. In a closed circuit, the path is complete.

quiz.q: Which is a conductor?
quiz.why: Copper is a metal, so it is a good conductor of electricity. Dry wood, plastic and glass are insulators.

quiz.q: The longer line in the cell symbol represents the
quiz.why: In the symbol of a cell, the longer thin line is the positive terminal and the shorter thick line is the negative terminal.

quiz.q: A fuse protects a circuit by
options: melting when current is too high
quiz.why: A fuse has a thin wire that melts when the current is too high, which breaks the circuit and protects appliances.

quiz.q: An electric bell works using the
quiz.why: An electric bell uses an electromagnet, which is the magnetic effect of current. The electromagnet pulls the hammer to strike the gong.

sources: NCERT Science Class 6–8 (Electricity and Circuits; Electric Current and its Effects) — topic reference

lessons.title: Magnets and the magnetic Earth

scenes.text: Aditi, 13, goes sailing on Chilika Lake with her grandfather, a retired naval officer. Fog rolls in and the shore disappears.
Grandpa takes out an old compass. The needle swings, then settles pointing north. 'The Earth itself is like a giant magnet,' he says.
They steer east by the compass and reach the jetty safely. That night Aditi makes her own compass with a magnetised needle floating on a leaf in water.

steps.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
steps.body:
**Magnetic materials** are attracted to magnets: **iron**, **nickel**, **cobalt** and many kinds of **steel**.
**Non-magnetic:** wood, plastic, paper, glass, rubber, and most other metals such as aluminium, copper, gold and silver.

Natural magnets: a rock called **magnetite** (lodestone). Most magnets we use are artificial: bar, horseshoe, ring, cylindrical.

steps.title: Poles
steps.body:
Every magnet has a **north pole (N)** and a **south pole (S)**. The attraction is strongest near the poles (iron filings cluster there).

- **Like poles repel** (N–N, S–S)
- **Unlike poles attract** (N–S)
- Poles always come in **pairs**: break a bar magnet in half and each piece has its own N and S.

**Repulsion is the sure test** of a magnet: a magnet can attract an unmagnetised iron bar, but only another magnet can repel it.

steps.title: Direction and the compass
steps.body:
A **freely suspended** bar magnet always comes to rest pointing roughly **north–south**. The end pointing north is the magnet's north (north-seeking) pole.

A **compass** is a small magnetised needle on a pivot. Travellers and sailors have used compasses for centuries.

The Earth behaves as if a giant magnet were inside it. Geographic north and magnetic north are close but not exactly at the same place.

steps.title: Making and caring for magnets
steps.body:
**Make a magnet:** stroke an iron nail or needle about 30–40 times from one end to the other with **one pole** of a bar magnet, lifting it away each time and always moving in the same direction.

**Or** wrap insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a cell — an **electromagnet** (see the electricity lesson).

**Magnets lose magnetism** if heated, hammered or dropped often. Store bar magnets in pairs with unlike poles side by side and pieces of soft iron (**keepers**) across the ends. Keep magnets away from phones, cards with magnetic strips and other electronics.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- 'All metals are magnetic' ✗ — aluminium cans and copper wires are not attracted.
- 'Attraction proves it's a magnet' ✗ — use repulsion.
- Small powerful magnets (like those in some toys) are dangerous if swallowed — keep them away from young children and seek medical help immediately if swallowed.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Magnetise a sewing needle by stroking it with a magnet. Push it through a small piece of cork or lay it on a leaf floating in a bowl of water. Which way does it point? Check with a phone compass app.

a.text: Your teacher gives you two identical-looking iron bars. Only one is a magnet. You have no other equipment. How do you find out which is the magnet?

choices.label: Bring one end of bar A near the end of bar B and see if they attract
choices.feedback: Attraction alone can't tell you — a magnet attracts plain iron too.

choices.label: Touch the end of bar A to the MIDDLE of bar B
choices.feedback: Clever — a magnet's middle has almost no pull.

b.text: They attract. But which one is the magnet? Now try something else.

choices.label: Touch the end of bar A to the middle of bar B
choices.feedback: Good thinking.

choices.label: Give up and guess
choices.feedback: Science beats guessing!

c.text: Bar A's end strongly attracts the middle of bar B. What does that tell you?

choices.label: Bar A is the magnet — its pole attracts plain iron anywhere
choices.feedback: Correct! If B were the magnet, its middle would barely attract.

choices.label: Bar B is the magnet
choices.feedback: A magnet's middle is nearly neutral, so B's middle wouldn't pull strongly.

end1.text: Brilliant! Bar A is the magnet. (With a second known magnet, repulsion would confirm it.)

end2.text: Key ideas: magnetism is strongest at the poles and weakest at the middle; repulsion only happens between two magnets.

quiz.q: Which is attracted by a magnet?
quiz.why: A magnet attracts iron, so an iron nail is attracted. Aluminium, plastic and copper are non-magnetic.

quiz.q: Two north poles brought together will
quiz.why: Like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart. Unlike poles attract.

quiz.q: A bar magnet is cut into two. Each piece has
quiz.why: Cutting a magnet always gives smaller magnets, each with both a north and a south pole. Poles cannot be separated.

quiz.q: The sure test of a magnet is
quiz.why: Only a magnet repels another magnet, while attraction also happens with iron. So repulsion is the sure test.

quiz.q: A freely suspended magnet points
quiz.why: A freely suspended magnet lines up in the north–south direction because of Earth's magnetism. This is how a compass works.

sources: NCERT Science Class 6 (Fun with Magnets) — topic reference

questions.q: Which of these is opaque?
questions.why: Cardboard blocks light, so it is opaque. Clear glass and water are transparent, and air lets light pass.

questions.q: Unlike magnetic poles
questions.why: Unlike (opposite) poles attract each other, so north and south poles attract. Like poles repel.

questions.q: A material that does not let current pass is an
questions.why: An insulator does not allow electric current to pass through it, like plastic or rubber. A conductor allows current.

questions.q: A plane-mirror image is
questions.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object. It cannot be caught on a screen.

questions.q: Which metal is magnetic?
questions.why: Nickel is a magnetic metal, like iron and cobalt. Gold, copper and aluminium are not magnetic.

questions.q: The device that breaks a circuit when current is too high is a
questions.why: A miniature circuit breaker (MCB) breaks a circuit when the current is too high, like a fuse, and it can be reset. A bulb or cell cannot do this.

questions.q: Vehicle side mirrors are convex because they
questions.why: A convex mirror gives a wider view of the traffic behind, though objects look smaller. It does not form real images or magnify.

questions.q: A ray makes 30° with the mirror surface. Angle of reflection?
questions.why: The angle of reflection is measured from the normal, which is perpendicular to the mirror. The ray makes 30° with the surface, so the angle with the normal is 90° − 30° = 60°.

questions.q: Electroplating uses the
questions.why: Electroplating uses the chemical effect of electric current, where current passing through a solution deposits a metal on an object.

questions.q: A rainbow forms by
questions.why: A rainbow forms when sunlight is dispersed (split into colours) by raindrops. It needs both sunlight and rain.

questions.q: Why do scientists draw circuit diagrams with symbols?
options: They show connections clearly and quickly
questions.why: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to show the connections clearly and quickly, and anyone can read them. The symbols do not conduct electricity.

questions.q: Someone is stuck to a live wire. First, you should
options: wait for them to let go
switch off the mains or use a dry wooden stick
questions.why: A person stuck to a live wire must not be touched directly, or you will get a shock too. Switch off the mains or push the person away with a dry wooden stick, then call for help (112).

questions.q: You stand 3 m from a plane mirror and walk 1 m towards it. Distance between you and your image now?
questions.why: At 3 m, you walk 1 m toward the mirror, so you are 2 m from it. The image is as far behind the mirror as you are in front, 2 m, so the distance between you and the image is 2 + 2 = 4 m.

courses.title: The Living World: cells, microbes, reproduction & growing up
courses.summary: Zoom into cells, meet the microorganisms that help and harm us, learn how plants and animals reproduce, and get a calm, factual overview of the changes of adolescence.
outcomes: Learners can describe cell structure and compare plant and animal cells
Learners can name groups of microorganisms with useful and harmful examples and ways to prevent disease and spoilage
Learners can explain asexual and sexual reproduction in plants and animals
Learners can describe the physical and emotional changes of puberty in all bodies and basic hygiene
Learners know where to get trustworthy help with questions about growing up
courses.guardianNote: This science course follows the middle-school (Class 6–8) syllabus. Lessons 1–3 cover cells, microorganisms and reproduction in plants and animals (fertilisation explained at the level of sperm, egg and zygote). Lesson 4 gives a factual, non-explicit overview of puberty for all genders — body changes, menstruation, wet dreams, hygiene, nutrition and feelings — in line with UNESCO's International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education (2018) for ages 9–12 and 12–15. No images beyond emoji are used. Learners are encouraged to talk to a parent, teacher or doctor, and are pointed to the Mann (wellbeing) school for deeper, gentle guidance.

lessons.title: Cells: the building blocks of life

scenes.text: In her school lab in Bhopal, Nikita peels a thin, see-through layer from an onion, puts it on a glass slide with a drop of water and a little stain.

Under the microscope she sees neat brick-like boxes, each with a dark dot. Her lab partner Ethan (from Canada) gently scrapes the inside of his cheek with a clean spoon — his cells look rounder, with no thick walls.
Their teacher Mrs Banerjee smiles: 'You've just seen what Robert Hooke started in 1665. Every living thing is made of cells.'

steps.title: What a cell is
steps.body:
The **cell** is the basic **structural and functional unit** of life — just as bricks build a house, cells build a body.

- **Robert Hooke** (1665) saw tiny compartments in thin slices of **cork** and named them 'cells'.
- **Unicellular** organisms are just one cell: amoeba, paramecium, bacteria.
- **Multicellular** organisms have many cells: plants, animals, us. An adult human has trillions of cells.

Cells come in many shapes and sizes. A nerve cell is long and branched to carry messages; a red blood cell is a disc for carrying oxygen; a muscle cell is long to contract.

steps.title: Parts of a cell
steps.body:
- **Cell membrane (plasma membrane):** a thin outer covering that controls what goes in and out.
- **Cytoplasm:** jelly-like fluid where many activities happen and where tiny structures (**organelles**) are found.
- **Nucleus:** usually round, the control centre. It contains **chromosomes**, which carry **genes** — instructions passed from parents to offspring.

Cells whose nucleus has a membrane around it are **eukaryotic** (plants, animals, fungi). **Bacteria** have no proper nuclear membrane — they are **prokaryotic**.

steps.title: Plant cell vs animal cell
steps.body:
**Only in plant cells:**
- a rigid **cell wall** (made of cellulose) outside the membrane, giving shape and protection
- **chloroplasts** with green **chlorophyll** for making food by photosynthesis
- usually one **large central vacuole**

**Animal cells:** no cell wall, no chloroplasts, small vacuoles (if any).

**Both** have: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria (release energy from food).

steps.title: From cells to organisms
steps.body:
**Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism**

- A **tissue** is a group of similar cells doing one job (muscle tissue).
- An **organ** is made of different tissues working together (heart, leaf).
- An **organ system** is a group of organs (the digestive system).

In the cell-explorer lab, tap each part of a plant and an animal cell to see what it does.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Animal cells have a cell wall' ✗ — only a membrane.
- 'The nucleus is in the vacuole' ✗ — it's in the cytoplasm.
- 'All cells are too small to see' — most are, but a hen's egg yolk is a single very large cell.
- In the lab: handle slides by the edges, lower the coverslip slowly to avoid air bubbles, and start with the lowest magnification.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw a plant cell and an animal cell side by side and label: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, chloroplast, vacuole. Colour only the parts that are unique to plants in green.

activity.prompt: Where is each part found?

quiz.q: Who first described 'cells', in cork?
quiz.why: Robert Hooke first described cells, in 1665, when he saw the tiny boxes in a slice of cork under a microscope.

quiz.q: The control centre of the cell is the
quiz.why: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It holds the chromosomes carrying genes.

quiz.q: Which is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
quiz.why: Chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis, are found in plant cells but not in animal cells.

quiz.q: Amoeba is
quiz.why: An amoeba is made of a single cell, so it is unicellular. Multicellular organisms like humans have many cells.

quiz.q: A group of similar cells doing the same job is a
quiz.why: A group of similar cells doing the same job forms a tissue. Tissues form organs and organs form systems.

sources: NCERT Science Class 8 (Cell — Structure and Functions) — topic reference

lessons.title: Microorganisms: friend and foe

story.title: Kiran's curd and her cousin's fever

scenes.text: In Kolhapur, Kiran watches her mother add a spoonful of old curd to warm milk. By morning the whole bowl has become curd.
The same week, her cousin Suresh gets a high fever with chills. The doctor tests his blood: malaria, spread by mosquitoes.
Kiran is amazed: tiny living things she can't see made the curd AND made Suresh ill. She sets out to learn which microbes help and which harm.

steps.title: The main groups
steps.body:
**Microorganisms (microbes)** are too small to see with the naked eye. Main groups:
- **Bacteria** — single cells, many shapes (rods, spheres, spirals)
- **Fungi** — yeasts (single-celled) and moulds (bread mould)
- **Protozoa** — single-celled, e.g. amoeba, paramecium
- **Algae** — e.g. chlamydomonas, spirogyra; they make their own food
- **Viruses** — even smaller; they can reproduce **only inside the cells of a host**. Whether they count as 'living' is debated, because outside a host they are inactive.

Microbes live everywhere: soil, water, air, hot springs, inside our gut.

steps.title: Useful microorganisms
steps.body:
- **Curd:** the bacterium *Lactobacillus* turns milk into curd.
- **Bread and idli/dosa batter:** **yeast** (and other microbes) produce carbon dioxide, making dough rise. This process is a kind of **fermentation**; yeast fermentation of sugar also produces alcohol.
- **Medicines:** **antibiotics** kill or stop bacteria. **Alexander Fleming** discovered penicillin from a mould in 1928.
- **Vaccines** train the body to fight specific diseases. **Edward Jenner** developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796. Thanks to vaccination, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.
- **Soil:** bacteria like *Rhizobium* in root nodules of peas, beans and other legumes fix nitrogen from air. Microbes also **decompose** dead plants and animals, recycling nutrients.

steps.title: Harmful microorganisms
steps.body:
Microbes that cause disease are called **pathogens**. Diseases that spread from person to person are **communicable**.

- **Bacteria:** tuberculosis (TB), cholera, typhoid
- **Viruses:** common cold, influenza, measles, chickenpox, polio, COVID-19
- **Protozoa:** malaria (*Plasmodium*, spread by the **female *Anopheles*** mosquito), amoebic dysentery

Some are spread by **carriers** — mosquitoes, houseflies. Microbes also spoil food (bad smell, mould) and cause plant diseases.

**Antibiotics do NOT work on viruses** like the cold or flu. Take antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them, and complete the course as advised.

steps.title: Prevention and food preservation
steps.body:
**Prevent disease:** wash hands with soap, drink boiled or purified water, cover food, don't let water stagnate (mosquito breeding), use nets/repellents, get vaccinated on schedule, cover your mouth when coughing.

**Preserve food** (slow microbial growth):
- **Salt** (pickles, fish), **sugar** (jams), **oil and vinegar** (pickles)
- **Refrigeration** (cold slows microbes)
- **Pasteurisation** — heating milk to about 70 °C for 15–30 seconds then cooling quickly (named after **Louis Pasteur**)
- **Drying, sealed packaging, chemical preservatives** (permitted limits only)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'All bacteria are bad' ✗ — most are harmless and many are essential.
- 'Antibiotics cure colds' ✗ — colds are viral.
- 'Fungi are plants' ✗ — they are a separate group and can't make their own food.
- Mouldy bread: throw it away — don't just scrape off the visible part.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Leave a slightly moist slice of bread in a closed box in a warm place for 3–4 days (then throw it away without opening it near your face). Observe the fuzzy mould through the box with a hand lens. What colour is it? This is a fungus growing from spores in the air.

activity.prompt: Match each microbe to what it does.

quiz.q: Malaria is caused by a
quiz.why: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan (a single-celled organism). It is not caused by a virus, bacterium or fungus.

quiz.q: Malaria is carried by the
quiz.why: Malaria is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito, which picks up the parasite from an infected person and passes it on.

quiz.q: Antibiotics are effective against
quiz.why: Antibiotics kill or stop the growth of bacteria. They do not work on viruses.

quiz.q: Pasteurisation involves
quiz.why: In pasteurisation, milk is heated to a suitable temperature to kill microbes and then cooled quickly to prevent new growth. It is not freezing or salting.

quiz.q: Who developed the smallpox vaccine?
quiz.why: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796. Fleming discovered penicillin and Hooke described cells.

sources: NCERT Science Class 8 (Microorganisms: Friend and Foe) — topic reference

lessons.title: Reproduction in plants and animals

story.title: Grandpa Tomar's potato and the frog pond

scenes.text: In a village near Meerut, Grandpa Tomar cuts an old potato into pieces, each with an 'eye', and plants them. Each grows into a new potato plant.
His granddaughter Simran notices bees visiting the mustard flowers. 'They're carrying pollen — that's how seeds form,' he says.
At the pond, they see a jelly-like mass of frog eggs. Weeks later: tadpoles, then tiny frogs. Simran realises living things make new ones in many different ways.

steps.title: Why reproduction matters
steps.body:
**Reproduction** is how living things produce **offspring** of their own kind. Without it, a species would die out.

Two main types:
- **Asexual:** one parent; offspring are (almost) identical copies.
- **Sexual:** two parents (or male and female parts); a male **gamete** and a female gamete join. Offspring show a mix of features — this **variation** helps species survive change.

steps.title: Asexual reproduction
steps.body:
- **Vegetative propagation** (new plants from roots, stems or leaves): potato 'eyes', ginger, rose stem cuttings, sugarcane, *Bryophyllum* leaf buds.
- **Budding:** a small bud grows on the parent and separates — **yeast**, **hydra**.
- **Fragmentation:** a piece breaks off and grows — **spirogyra** (alga).
- **Spore formation:** tiny spores spread by air and grow in moist conditions — **bread mould**, ferns, mosses.
- **Binary fission:** one cell splits into two — **amoeba**, bacteria.

steps.title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
steps.body:
Flower parts:
- **Stamen** (male): **anther** (makes **pollen**) on a **filament**
- **Pistil** (female): **stigma**, **style** and **ovary** (contains **ovules** with the egg cell)

Steps:
1. **Pollination:** pollen reaches the stigma — the same flower (**self-pollination**) or another flower of the same kind (**cross-pollination**) by insects, wind, water or birds.
2. **Fertilisation:** the male cell joins the egg cell → **zygote** → grows into an **embryo**.
3. The **ovule becomes the seed**; the **ovary becomes the fruit**.
4. **Seed dispersal** by wind (cotton, drumstick), water (coconut), animals (burrs, eaten fruits) or bursting pods.

steps.title: Sexual reproduction in animals
steps.body:
Males produce **sperm** (in the **testes**); females produce **eggs/ova** (in the **ovaries**). When a sperm and an egg fuse — **fertilisation** — a single cell called the **zygote** forms. It divides again and again to form an **embryo**.

- **Internal fertilisation** (inside the female's body): humans, cows, dogs, hens.
- **External fertilisation** (outside, usually in water): frogs, most fish. They release many eggs because many are lost.

- **Viviparous** animals give birth to young ones (humans, cows, dogs).
- **Oviparous** animals lay eggs (hens, frogs, lizards, butterflies).

**Metamorphosis:** big changes after hatching — egg → tadpole → frog; egg → larva → pupa → adult in silkworms and butterflies. In humans, the embryo develops in the mother's **uterus** (womb); once it has recognisable body features, it's called a **foetus**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The seed becomes the fruit' ✗ — the **ovary** becomes the fruit, the **ovule** becomes the seed.
- 'All animals lay eggs or all give birth' — it depends on the species.
- 'Pollination = fertilisation' ✗ — pollination is pollen transfer; fertilisation is the fusing of gametes, which comes after.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Place a *Bryophyllum* (patharchatta) leaf on moist soil, or a piece of money-plant stem in water. Watch for 2 weeks. Keep a diary with dates and sketches of new roots and shoots.

activity.prompt: Put the stages of seed formation in a flowering plant in order.
items: Anther releases pollen grains
Pollen lands on the stigma (pollination)
The male cell reaches the ovule
Male and female cells fuse (fertilisation) to form a zygote
The zygote grows into an embryo inside the seed
The ovary ripens into a fruit

quiz.q: Yeast reproduces asexually by
quiz.why: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding: a small bud grows on the parent cell and then separates. It does not use seeds or pollination.

quiz.q: The female part of a flower is the
quiz.why: The pistil is the female part of a flower, made of the stigma, style and ovary. The stamen, with anther and filament, is the male part.

quiz.q: After fertilisation, the ovary becomes the
quiz.why: After fertilisation the ovary grows into the fruit, and the ovule becomes the seed.

quiz.q: Frogs have
quiz.why: Frogs show external fertilisation: the female lays eggs in water and the male releases sperm over them outside the body.

quiz.q: The cell formed when a sperm and an egg fuse is the
quiz.why: When a sperm and an egg fuse, they form a single cell called a zygote. The zygote divides to form the embryo.

sources: NCERT Science Class 7–8 (Reproduction in Plants; Reproduction in Animals) — topic reference

lessons.title: Growing up: puberty and adolescence

scenes.text: Anu, 12, got her first period at school and felt scared and embarrassed. Her classmate Rahul, 13, woke up one morning after a wet dream and worried something was wrong with him.
Neither told anyone for days. Then their science teacher, Mrs Thomas, taught the class about adolescence — calmly, with real words and no giggling.
Anu and Rahul both realised: what happened to them is normal, healthy and expected. Anu talked to her mother; Rahul talked to his uncle. Both felt lighter.

steps.title: Adolescence and puberty
steps.body:
**Adolescence** is the time between childhood and adulthood — roughly **10 to 19 years** of age.

**Puberty** is the part of adolescence when the body becomes physically mature and capable of reproduction. It is triggered by **hormones** — chemical messengers released by glands. The **pituitary gland** in the brain signals the **testes** to make **testosterone** and the **ovaries** to make **oestrogen** (and progesterone).

Everyone's timing is different. Puberty often starts between about **8 and 13 in girls** and **9 and 14 in boys**. Earlier or later than friends is usually normal — if you're worried, ask a doctor.

steps.title: Changes for everyone
steps.body:
- **Growth spurt:** you may grow taller quickly; arms and legs can seem to grow first.
- **Hair** grows in the armpits and the genital (pubic) area.
- **Sweat glands** become more active → body odour; **oil glands** → pimples (acne).
- **Emotions:** mood swings, stronger feelings, wanting more privacy and independence, new interest or attractions — all common.
- **Thinking:** you can reason more deeply and question things.

steps.title: Changes in girls and in boys
steps.body:
**Girls (often first):** breasts develop, hips widen, and **menstruation** begins (the first period is called **menarche**). Each month the lining of the uterus thickens to prepare for a possible pregnancy; if no egg is fertilised, the lining comes out through the vagina as blood over a few days. Cycles are often irregular in the first year or two; many cycles are between about 21 and 35 days. Use sanitary pads, menstrual cups or clean cloth, change regularly, and wash hands.

**Boys:** shoulders broaden, muscles grow, the **voice deepens** (it may 'crack' for a while) and the **Adam's apple** (larynx) becomes noticeable, facial hair grows. The testes begin making sperm, and **nocturnal emissions (wet dreams)** — release of semen during sleep — are common and **completely normal**. Nothing needs to be done except change and wash.

These changes happen in **every** healthy body at its own pace — they are nothing to be ashamed of.

steps.title: Taking care of yourself
steps.body:
- **Hygiene:** bathe daily, wash armpits and private parts with water and mild soap, wear clean cotton underwear, change pads regularly during periods.
- **Nutrition:** your body is building bone and muscle — eat protein, calcium (milk, curd, ragi) and **iron** (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates, pulses, meat/eggs if you eat them). Iron matters especially once periods start.
- **Activity and sleep:** aim for daily exercise and around 8–10 hours of sleep.
- **Say no** to tobacco, alcohol and drugs — they harm a growing body and brain.
- **Pimples:** wash your face gently twice a day; don't squeeze them (it can scar).

steps.title: Myths, feelings and getting help
steps.body:
**Myths — all false:** a girl on her period is 'impure' or shouldn't go to school, play or enter the kitchen; wet dreams weaken the body; the timing of your puberty says something about your character.

**Feelings:** stress, worry about looks and comparing yourself to others are common. Talk to someone you trust — a parent, older sibling, teacher, school counsellor or doctor.

**Your body belongs to you.** No one should touch you in a way that makes you uncomfortable or ask you to keep it secret. Tell a trusted adult, or call **1098** (Childline) or **112** in an emergency.

For gentle, deeper answers to questions people don't usually ask aloud, visit the **Mann** (wellbeing) school.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- No signs of puberty at all by about 13 (girls) or 14 (boys)
- Periods that are extremely heavy (soaking a pad every hour), very painful, or last more than about 7 days
- No period by 15, or periods stopping for several months after they had started
- Pain or swelling in the testes (go immediately)
- Feeling very low, anxious or hopeless for weeks — **Tele-MANAS 14416** is free

This is general education, not medical advice.

activity.prompt: Questions many teens wonder about but don't ask

items.q: I got my first period in class. What should I do?
items.a: Stay calm — it happens to millions of girls. Ask a female teacher, the school nurse or a friend for a pad. Tie a jacket or sweater around your waist if your clothes are stained. Tell your parent or guardian later so you can be prepared next time. Many schools keep spare pads.

items.q: Is it normal to have a wet dream?
items.a: Yes. Nocturnal emission is a normal part of puberty for boys. It is not an illness, it doesn't weaken you, and it's not something you did wrong. Just wash and change your clothes.

items.q: My friends have grown taller and I haven't. Is something wrong?
items.a: Usually not. Puberty can start years apart in healthy people. If you have no signs of puberty by about 13–14, or you are worried, a doctor can check.

items.q: Why do I feel angry or sad for no reason?
items.a: Hormone changes, more stress and less sleep can all affect moods. Exercise, sleep, talking to someone and writing your feelings down help. If low moods last for weeks, talk to a trusted adult or a counsellor.

items.q: Is it okay to bathe or play sports during my period?
items.a: Yes. Bathing is good hygiene and exercise can even ease cramps. There is no medical reason to stop normal activities.

quiz.q: The age range usually called adolescence is about
quiz.why: Adolescence is usually taken as the period from about 10 to 19 years, when children grow into adults.

quiz.q: Puberty is triggered by
quiz.why: Puberty is triggered by hormones, such as testosterone in boys and oestrogen in girls. They cause body changes.

quiz.q: Wet dreams (nocturnal emissions) are
quiz.why: Wet dreams are a normal part of growing up for boys during puberty, and they are not a disease or a sign of weakness.

quiz.q: During menstruation, it is fine to
quiz.why: Menstruation is a normal body process, so girls can go to school, play and do their usual activities. They should eat well and keep clean.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is especially important for adolescent girls once periods begin?
quiz.why: Iron is especially important for adolescent girls once periods start, because monthly blood loss increases the need for iron. Lack of it can cause anaemia.

sources: NCERT Science Class 8 (Reaching the Age of Adolescence) — topic reference
UNESCO ITGSE 2018
WHO adolescent health

questions.q: The basic unit of life is the
questions.why: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, since all living things are made of cells. Atoms are too small and tissues and organs are made of cells.

questions.q: Curd is made from milk with the help of

questions.why: Measles is caused by a virus. Typhoid and cholera are bacterial diseases, and malaria is caused by a protozoan.

questions.why: Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans, and fix nitrogen from the air. Rice, wheat and mango do not have them.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of organisation?
questions.why: The correct order of organisation is cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system. Cells are the smallest unit.

questions.q: Why don't antibiotics help with a common cold?

Timing varies widely and is usually normal
questions.why: Puberty timing varies widely among healthy people, so being earlier or later is usually normal. Menstruation is a normal process, not illness, and both boys and girls go through puberty.

questions.why: A bacterium has no nuclear membrane, so its genetic material lies loose in the cell. It is a prokaryote, while amoeba, cheek and onion cells have a true nucleus.

lessons.title: The Harappan cities

scenes.text: On a school trip to Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, Meher walks along stone-lined channels built about 4,500 years ago.
The guide, Mr Solanki, shows huge water reservoirs. 'This city stored every drop of rain. Its people were expert planners.'
Meher asks what the people wrote. 'They had a script on their seals,' he says, 'but nobody has deciphered it yet.' History, Meher realises, is also about what we don't know.

steps.title: How do we know about the past?
steps.body:
Historians use **sources**:
- **Archaeological sources:** buildings, pots, tools, coins, bones, seals — found by careful digging (**excavation**).
- **Inscriptions:** writing on hard surfaces like stone or metal.
- **Manuscripts:** handwritten books, often on palm leaf or birch bark.

Dates: **BCE** (Before Common Era) counts backwards — 500 BCE is earlier than 200 BCE. **CE** (Common Era) counts forwards. (Older books use BC and AD.)

steps.title: A civilisation of planned cities
steps.body:
The **Harappan civilisation** (also called the Indus Valley or Indus–Sarasvati civilisation) was at its height roughly **4,500 to 3,900 years ago** (about 2600–1900 BCE). It is named after **Harappa** (now in Pakistan), the first site to be found, about a hundred years ago.

Important sites: **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-daro** (Pakistan); **Lothal** and **Dholavira** (Gujarat); **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan); **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana).

Features:
- Cities in two parts: a raised **citadel** and a larger **lower town**
- Straight streets crossing at right angles, houses of **baked bricks** of standard proportions
- **Covered drains** along streets — one of the best drainage systems of the ancient world
- The **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro, a watertight tank, perhaps for special ceremonies
- **Granaries**, a **dockyard** at Lothal, and Dholavira's water reservoirs

steps.title: Life, crafts and trade
steps.body:
- **Farming:** wheat, barley, pulses, cotton; they kept cattle, sheep and goats.
- **Crafts:** beads of carnelian, stone weights, copper and bronze tools, pottery with black designs, cotton cloth.
- **Seals:** small stone squares with animals (like a humped bull or unicorn-like animal) and short lines of a **script that is still undeciphered**.
- **Trade:** with distant lands, including Mesopotamia (in present-day Iraq).

Around 3,900 years ago, many cities were gradually abandoned. Historians suggest several possible reasons — rivers drying or changing course, floods, deforestation — but there is **no single agreed answer**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying we can 'read' Harappan writing — we can't yet.
- Thinking all Harappan sites are in India — Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are in Pakistan today; modern borders did not exist then.
- Treating a guess as fact: 'The Great Bath was definitely a temple' — historians say 'possibly'. Good historians separate evidence from interpretation.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Imagine an archaeologist digs up your home 4,000 years from now. Which five objects would survive, and what would they guess about your life? Would any guess be wrong?

quiz.why: Writing carved on hard surfaces like stone or metal is called an inscription. A manuscript is handwritten on material like palm leaf or paper.

quiz.why: Historians suggest several reasons for the decline of Harappan cities, such as climate change, river shifts and loss of trade, but none is certain. The script is still undeciphered.

lessons.title: Vedas, kingdoms, the Buddha and Mahavira

scenes.text: In Prayagraj, Arjun's grandmother chants a verse she learnt as a child. 'This is from the Rigveda,' she says. 'It was passed on by memory for many centuries before anyone wrote it down.'
At school, Arjun's teacher Mr Yadav tells how small chiefdoms grew into large kingdoms called mahajanapadas, with forts, armies and taxes.
He also tells of a prince who left his palace to find why people suffer — Siddhartha, who became the Buddha. Arjun wonders: why did so many new ideas arise at the same time?

steps.title: The Vedas
steps.body:
The **Rigveda** is one of the oldest texts in the world, composed roughly **3,500 years ago** in an early form of **Sanskrit**. It has over a thousand hymns praising deities such as **Agni** (fire), **Indra** and **Soma**.

There are four Vedas: **Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva**. They were memorised and recited with great accuracy and written down much later.

The hymns mention cattle, horses, chariots, rivers such as the Sindhu and Sarasvati, and groups called **jana**.

steps.title: From janapadas to mahajanapadas
steps.body:
Around **2,500 years ago**, some janapadas grew powerful and became **mahajanapadas** ('great janapadas') — Buddhist and Jaina texts list **sixteen**.

- Many had capitals with **fortified walls**.
- Rulers kept **armies** and collected **taxes** on crops, crafts, trade and herding.
- **Magadha** (in present-day Bihar) became the strongest, helped by rivers, forests (elephants for the army), and iron ore. Its capital was **Rajagriha** (Rajgir), later **Pataliputra** (Patna).
- **Vajji**, with its capital Vaishali, was a **gana** or **sangha** — power was shared by many rulers who met in assemblies.

steps.title: The Buddha
steps.body:
**Siddhartha Gautama**, a prince of the Sakya gana, lived about 2,500 years ago.
- He left home to seek answers about suffering and gained **enlightenment** under a peepal tree at **Bodh Gaya** (Bihar).
- He gave his **first sermon at Sarnath**, near Varanasi.
- He taught that **tanha** (craving) causes unhappiness, and that a middle path of moderation, kindness and respect for life leads to peace.
- He taught in **Prakrit**, the language of ordinary people, so everyone could understand.

His followers formed the **sangha**, communities of monks and nuns.

steps.title: Mahavira and the Upanishads
steps.body:
**Vardhamana Mahavira**, of the Vajji sangha, was the 24th and last **tirthankara** of the Jainas. He taught that people should not harm any living being (**ahimsa**), and practised strict self-discipline. His teachings were also in Prakrit.

Around the same time, thinkers composed the **Upanishads**, asking questions about life after death and the idea of **atman** (individual soul) and **brahman** (universal soul).

This period is a remarkable time of **questioning** in Indian history.

steps.title: Careful with dates
steps.body: Dates for this period are **approximate**. Historians write 'about 2,500 years ago' or 'c. 6th–5th century BCE' (c. = circa, 'around'). Different books may give slightly different years — that's normal.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: The Buddha and Mahavira chose to teach in the everyday language rather than a scholarly one. Write two sentences on why that choice mattered. Who might have been left out otherwise?

activity.prompt: Match the place to its connection.

quiz.why: The Rigveda was composed in an early form of Sanskrit, called Vedic Sanskrit. It is the oldest of the Vedas.

quiz.why: Magadha was the most powerful mahajanapada, helped by its rivers, forests with elephants and iron ore.

quiz.why: Mahavira taught ahimsa, which means not harming any living being. Jainism stresses non-violence.

options: Prakrit, the language of ordinary people
quiz.why: The Buddha taught in Prakrit, the language of ordinary people, so that everyone could understand his message.

quiz.why: In a gana or sangha, power was shared by many rulers, who took decisions in assemblies, unlike in a monarchy with a single king.

lessons.title: The Mauryas and Ashoka

scenes.text: Tara in Bhubaneswar notices four lions on the back of a ₹10 coin. 'Why lions?' she asks her father.
He takes her to the museum, where a guide explains: 'It's the national emblem, adapted from the Lion Capital that Emperor Ashoka placed at Sarnath.'
'And the battlefield of Kalinga, where Ashoka changed his ways, is very near here — in Odisha.' Tara is amazed that history is under her feet.

steps.title: Founding the empire
steps.body:
About **2,300 years ago** (around 321 BCE), **Chandragupta Maurya** founded the **Mauryan empire**, with its capital at **Pataliputra**. He was supported by a wise adviser, **Chanakya** (also called **Kautilya**), whose ideas are recorded in the **Arthashastra**, a book about government, taxes and running a state.

**Megasthenes**, a Greek ambassador, lived at Chandragupta's court and wrote about Pataliputra.

Chandragupta's grandson **Ashoka** became the most famous Mauryan ruler.

steps.title: The Kalinga war
steps.body:
Ashoka fought a war to conquer **Kalinga** (in present-day coastal Odisha), around 261 BCE. He won — but in his own inscriptions he describes his deep sorrow at the huge loss of life.

After this, Ashoka **gave up wars of conquest** — he is one of very few rulers in history to do so after a victory.

steps.title: Ashoka's dhamma
steps.body:
Ashoka's **dhamma** (from Sanskrit 'dharma') was a set of moral ideas for everyone, not a new religion or god:
- be kind to slaves and servants
- respect elders, teachers and priests (brahmins and monks)
- be compassionate to all creatures
- respect other people's religions and traditions

He appointed **dhamma mahamattas** (officials) to spread the message, and had it carved on **rocks and pillars** across the subcontinent. Most inscriptions are in **Prakrit**, mostly in the **Brahmi** script. He also sent messengers to other lands, including Sri Lanka.

steps.title: Ashoka in modern India
steps.body:
- India's **national emblem** is adapted from the **Lion Capital of Sarnath**; it is used on coins, notes and government documents.
- The **Ashoka Chakra** (a 24-spoked wheel) is in the centre of the national flag.

The Mauryan empire lasted roughly 150 years. After it, kingdoms such as those of the **Kushanas** in the north-west and the **Satavahanas** in the Deccan rose.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up **Chandragupta Maurya** (Mauryan, c. 321 BCE) with **Chandragupta I** and **II** (Gupta dynasty, centuries later).
- Saying dhamma was a new religion — it was a moral code.
- Thinking the empire covered all of present-day India — it did not include the far south.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a short 'inscription' (3–4 lines) of rules for kindness in your school, in Ashoka's style. Begin: 'Thus says…'.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order (earliest first).

quiz.why: Kalinga, which Ashoka fought, is in present-day Odisha, on the eastern coast.

quiz.why: India's national emblem is taken from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, which has four lions standing back to back.

lessons.title: The Gupta age and southern kingdoms

scenes.text: At the Qutb complex in Delhi, Rhea and her friend Kenji (visiting from Japan) find an iron pillar over 7 metres tall.
A sign says it is about 1,600 years old — from the Gupta period — and has barely rusted. Kenji, who loves chemistry, is amazed.
Rhea adds: 'And from the same age came Aryabhata, who said the Earth spins on its axis.' Science, art and literature flourished together.

steps.title: The Guptas
steps.body:
The **Gupta dynasty** began around **320 CE** with **Chandragupta I**.
- **Samudragupta** is known from a **prashasti** (a poem of praise) by his court poet **Harishena**, inscribed on the Ashokan pillar at **Prayagraj** (Allahabad). It lists his conquests.
- **Chandragupta II** was a patron of poets and scholars.

Often called a 'classical' age because of its remarkable art, literature and science. (Historians remind us that 'golden age' praise reflects mainly the lives of the rich — ordinary people's lives were often harder.)

steps.title: Science, literature and learning
steps.body:
- **Aryabhata** wrote the **Aryabhatiya** (499 CE). He explained that day and night are caused by the **Earth rotating** on its axis, gave a scientific explanation of **eclipses**, and calculated the value of **π** quite accurately.
- The use of **zero** and the place-value system with nine digits was being developed in India in this period; it later spread to the world through Arab scholars.
- **Kalidasa** wrote famous Sanskrit works such as *Abhijnana Shakuntalam* and *Meghaduta*.
- **Nalanda** in Bihar became a great centre of learning (from around the 5th century CE), later visited by the Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** in the 7th century.
- **Metalwork:** the rust-resistant **iron pillar** at Mehrauli.
- **Art:** the famous paintings and sculptures at **Ajanta** (Maharashtra).

steps.title: Kingdoms of the south and Harsha
steps.body:
- **Sangam literature** — some of the oldest Tamil poems — describes three ruling families: the **Cholas**, **Cheras** and **Pandyas**.
- The **Pallavas** ruled around **Kanchipuram**; their stone temples at **Mahabalipuram** are famous.
- The **Chalukyas** ruled from around **Aihole** and Badami in Karnataka. The Chalukya king **Pulakeshin II** stopped the advance of **Harshavardhana** of Kanauj in the 7th century.
- **Harsha's** life was written by his court poet **Banabhatta** in the *Harshacharita*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Aryabhata 'invented zero' — the zero and place-value system developed over time in India; give credit carefully.
- Confusing the **Gupta** Chandraguptas with **Chandragupta Maurya**.
- Thinking prashastis are neutral — they were written to **praise** a king, so historians read them carefully.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A prashasti praises a ruler. Write a short 'prashasti' for someone you admire (a grandparent, a teacher). Then write one honest line that a prashasti would leave out. What does this teach you about sources?

quiz.why: Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, wrote the prashasti (a praise poem) engraved on the Allahabad pillar.

quiz.why: A prashasti was written to praise the king, so it may exaggerate. Historians should read it carefully and check it against other evidence.

questions.q: BCE dates count
questions.why: BCE dates count backwards toward year 1, so a larger BCE number means an earlier time. 500 BCE is earlier than 200 BCE.

questions.q: Harappan cities had
questions.why: Harappan cities had covered drains along the streets, which shows careful planning. They had no printing presses, railways or skyscrapers.

questions.q: The Buddha gained enlightenment at
questions.why: The Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, sitting under a peepal tree. Lumbini is his birthplace and Sarnath is where he gave his first sermon.

questions.q: The oldest of the four Vedas is the
questions.why: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas, composed around 3,500 years ago. The Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas came later.

questions.q: The Mauryan capital was
questions.why: Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan empire. It is in present-day Bihar, near Patna.

questions.q: Ashoka gave up wars of conquest after
questions.why: Ashoka gave up wars of conquest after the Kalinga war because he felt sorry about the suffering it caused. His inscriptions express this sorrow.

questions.q: Lothal is in
questions.why: Lothal, a Harappan site with a dockyard, is in Gujarat. It is not in Tamil Nadu, Punjab or Bihar.

questions.q: Megasthenes was a
questions.why: Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent to the court of Chandragupta Maurya, and he wrote about India. He was not a Chinese pilgrim or Mughal noble.

questions.q: Which is NOT a source used by historians?
options: A modern film made only for entertainment
questions.why: Inscriptions, coins and manuscripts are sources used by historians. A modern film made only for entertainment is not evidence from the period.

questions.q: Magadha grew powerful partly because of
options: rivers, forests with elephants and iron ore
questions.why: Magadha grew powerful partly because it had rivers for transport and farming, forests with elephants for the army and iron ore for tools and weapons.

questions.q: The Harappan script
questions.why: The Harappan script has not yet been deciphered, so we cannot read what the seals say. It is not the same as Brahmi.

questions.q: Which order is correct (earliest first)?
questions.why: The Harappans were first (around 2600 BCE), then the Mauryas (around 321 BCE), then the Guptas (around 320 CE). Earlier dates come first in order.

questions.q: A historian finds a prashasti that says a king 'was never defeated'. The best response is to
questions.why: A prashasti was written to praise the king, so a claim that he was never defeated should be compared with other sources. Accepting it fully or ignoring it are both mistakes.

questions.q: Ashoka's inscriptions were mostly in Prakrit rather than Sanskrit because
options: he wanted ordinary people to understand
questions.why: Ashoka wrote in Prakrit, which ordinary people spoke, because he wanted them to understand his message. Sanskrit existed but was used by scholars.

courses.summary: From about 700 to 1750 CE: the Cholas and other regional kingdoms, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughal empire, Vijayanagara, and the devotional and cultural traditions that shaped everyday life.

lessons.title: New kingdoms and the Cholas

scenes.text: In Thanjavur, Selvi looks up at the towering vimana of the Brihadeeswara temple, completed over 1,000 years ago.
Her grandfather shows inscriptions carved on the walls. 'These tell us about the king Rajaraja Chola and the gifts made to the temple.'
'His son Rajendra sent ships across the sea to Southeast Asia,' Grandpa adds. Selvi imagines sails on the Bay of Bengal.

steps.title: A time of many kingdoms
steps.body:
Between about **700 and 1200 CE**, many regional kingdoms rose and fell: the **Rashtrakutas** in the Deccan, the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** in the north-west, the **Palas** in Bengal, and the **Cholas** in the south, among others.

They often fought over rich areas such as **Kanauj** in the Ganga valley — historians call this the **tripartite struggle** among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas.

Rulers gave land grants (recorded on **copper plates**) and built temples, which were also centres of economic and social life.

steps.title: The Chola empire
steps.body:
- **Rajaraja I** (ruled c. 985–1014 CE) built a powerful kingdom and the **Rajarajeshvara** (Brihadeeswara) temple at **Thanjavur**.
- His son **Rajendra I** sent armies to the Ganga valley and a **naval expedition** to Southeast Asia. He built a new capital, **Gangaikonda Cholapuram**.
- Cholas were famous for **bronze sculptures** made by the lost-wax method — such as images of **Nataraja**.
- **Agriculture:** they built tanks, wells and canals; the Kaveri delta was fertile.
- **Village assemblies:** inscriptions from **Uttaramerur** (Tamil Nadu) describe how members of a **sabha** were chosen — by writing names on palm leaves and drawing lots, with rules about who could stand.

steps.title: What 'medieval' means
steps.body:
Historians divide the past into periods to study it. 'Medieval' (middle) roughly covers **700–1750 CE** in Indian history books.

Older British-era writers divided Indian history by the religion of rulers ('Hindu', 'Muslim', 'British') — historians today reject this, because it ignores the variety of people, economies and cultures, and wrongly suggests that only rulers' religion mattered.

New sources in this period: **paper** became more common, so we have more manuscripts, chronicles and records.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a whole period by one religion — historians avoid this.
- Thinking kingdoms had fixed borders like countries today — borders moved with wars and alliances.
- Confusing the Chola temple (Thanjavur) with Pallava temples (Mahabalipuram).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: The Uttaramerur sabha used lots to pick members. Compare this with how your class monitor is chosen. List one advantage and one disadvantage of each method.

activity.prompt: Match the kingdom or person to the fact.

quiz.q: The Brihadeeswara temple is in
quiz.why: The Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur was built by the Chola king Rajaraja I. It is a famous example of Chola architecture.

quiz.q: Copper plates were often used to record
quiz.why: Rulers recorded land grants on copper plates, so historians use them to learn about villages and donations.

quiz.q: The 'tripartite struggle' was mainly over
quiz.why: The tripartite struggle was fought by the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas for control of Kanauj, an important city in the Ganga valley.

quiz.q: Why do historians avoid calling periods 'Hindu' or 'Muslim'?
options: It ignores the variety of people and life
Because the period had no religion
quiz.why: Historians avoid labelling periods as 'Hindu' or 'Muslim' because this ignores the variety of people, society, economy and culture in each age.

lessons.title: The Delhi Sultanate

scenes.text: Ishaan in Delhi climbs the hill near Mehrauli with his history-loving aunt Farah to look at the Qutb Minar.
'Qutbuddin Aibak began it, and Iltutmish added more storeys,' she explains. 'Different rulers kept building — like chapters in a book.'
'And Iltutmish's daughter Raziyya became Sultan herself.' Ishaan is surprised — a woman ruler 800 years ago!

steps.title: Delhi becomes a capital
steps.body:
Delhi first became an important capital under the **Tomara** and **Chauhan** (Chahamana) Rajputs. **Prithviraj Chauhan** ruled in the late 12th century.

From the early **13th century**, the **Delhi Sultans** ruled from Delhi. Five dynasties followed one another: **Mamluk ('Slave'), Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi**. The Sultanate lasted until **1526**.

steps.title: Key rulers
steps.body:
- **Qutbuddin Aibak** — began the **Qutb Minar**; often given as the first Sultan (from 1206).
- **Iltutmish** — strengthened the Sultanate; completed more of the Qutb Minar.
- **Raziyya** (Razia) — Iltutmish's daughter, ruled **1236–1240**. Chroniclers of the time accepted she was able, but nobles resisted a woman ruler and she was removed.
- **Alauddin Khalji** — defended against **Mongol** attacks, kept a large standing army paid in cash, and **controlled prices** in Delhi's markets.
- **Muhammad bin Tughluq** — shifted the capital to **Daulatabad** in the Deccan and introduced a **token currency** in copper; both plans ran into serious problems. The traveller **Ibn Battuta** from Morocco visited his court.

steps.title: How the Sultans governed
steps.body:
- Lands were given to military commanders as **iqtas**; the holder (**iqtadar** or **muqti**) collected revenue and kept troops.
- Revenue came mainly from **land tax** on peasants.
- Persian became the language of administration.
- Mosques such as the **Quwwat al-Islam** in Delhi and the city of **Jahanpanah** were built.

In **1526**, **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at the **First Battle of Panipat**, ending the Sultanate and founding Mughal rule.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Sultanate controlled all of India all the time — its control rose and fell; many regions were independent.
- Treating one chronicle as the whole truth — chroniclers often wrote for the Sultan, praising him.

steps.body: Muhammad bin Tughluq's token copper coins failed partly because many people forged them. Today our coins and notes have security features. Look at a ₹100 note: list three features that make forging difficult.

lessons.title: The Mughal empire

story.title: Zainab's school trip to Fatehpur Sikri

scenes.text: Zainab from Agra visits Fatehpur Sikri, the red-sandstone city built by Akbar.
In the Ibadat Khana area, the guide says Akbar invited scholars of many faiths to discuss religion. Zainab's friend Jasmine, a Christian, is surprised to hear that Jesuit priests came too.
Back in Agra, they see the Taj Mahal glowing at sunset — built by Akbar's grandson Shah Jahan. Two buildings, two emperors, one long story.

steps.title: The great Mughals
steps.body:
- **Babur** (1526–1530) — founded the empire after Panipat.
- **Humayun** — lost his kingdom to the Afghan ruler **Sher Shah Suri** (known for roads, the rupiya coin and administration) and regained it in 1555.
- **Akbar** (1556–1605) — expanded and organised the empire.
- **Jahangir** (1605–1627)
- **Shah Jahan** (1627–1658) — built the **Taj Mahal** in Agra and the city of **Shahjahanabad** in Delhi with the **Red Fort**.
- **Aurangzeb** (1658–1707) — the empire reached its largest size, but long wars in the Deccan strained it.

After **1707**, regional powers grew stronger and Mughal power declined.

steps.title: Akbar's administration
steps.body:
- **Mansabdari system:** nobles (**mansabdars**) held ranks (**zat**) that fixed their salary and the number of cavalrymen (**sawar**) they had to keep. Their pay was often given as revenue from land assignments called **jagirs**.
- **Land revenue:** under **Todar Mal**, land was surveyed and revenue fixed on crops (the **zabt** system).
- The empire was divided into **subas** (provinces) under **subadars**.
- **Sulh-i kul** ('universal peace'): Akbar's policy of tolerance — he did not discriminate between religions and emphasised justice and peace. He abolished the **jizya** tax on non-Muslims.
- His court historian **Abul Fazl** wrote the **Akbarnama** and **Ain-i Akbari**.

steps.title: Mughal legacy
steps.body:
- **Architecture:** Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort (all UNESCO World Heritage Sites), with **charbagh** (four-part) gardens.
- **Miniature painting**, music and Persian and Hindavi literature flourished.
- Many words in Hindi and Urdu, foods and clothing styles grew from this blending of cultures.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'Mughal' rulers were all the same — policies differed a great deal between emperors.
- Confusing **jagir** (revenue assignment) with **mansab** (rank).
- Saying Akbar founded the empire — **Babur** did.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Akbar invited people of different beliefs to debate respectfully. Hold a 5-minute class 'Ibadat Khana' on a harmless topic (e.g. 'Is homework useful?'). Rule: you must summarise the other side fairly before you reply.

a.text: You are a young historian. One Mughal chronicle praises an emperor as 'loved by all'. A peasant petition from the same year complains of very high taxes. What do you do?

choices.label: Trust the chronicle — it was written by an educated court historian
choices.feedback: Court historians wrote for the emperor; they had reasons to praise.

choices.label: Compare both sources and look for more evidence
choices.feedback: That's how historians work.

b.text: Your teacher asks: 'Who paid the court historian?' Do you want to reconsider?

choices.label: Yes — compare it with other sources
choices.feedback: Good — always ask who wrote a source and why.

choices.label: No — chronicles are always right
choices.feedback: That leads to one-sided history.

c.text: You find revenue records showing tax rose that year after a drought. What is the best conclusion?

choices.label: Court life may have been grand, while peasants faced hardship that year
choices.feedback: A balanced conclusion using several sources.

choices.label: The emperor was evil
choices.feedback: That jumps beyond the evidence.

end1.text: Excellent! You used multiple sources, asked who wrote them and why, and reached a conclusion the evidence supports.

end2.text: Remember: every source has an author with a point of view. Compare sources and don't claim more than the evidence shows.

quiz.q: Who defeated Humayun for a time?
quiz.why: Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun and forced him out for some years. Humayun returned and regained the throne in 1555.

options: a noble with a military-civil rank
quiz.why: A mansabdar was a noble with a rank (mansab) in the Mughal system, with both military and civil duties. The rank fixed his salary and soldiers.

quiz.q: Sulh-i kul means
quiz.why: 'Sulh-i kul' means universal peace, Akbar's policy of tolerance toward all religions.

quiz.q: The Taj Mahal was built by
quiz.why: The Taj Mahal in Agra was built by Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

quiz.q: The Akbarnama was written by
quiz.why: The Akbarnama was written by Abul Fazl, Akbar's court historian, and it records Akbar's reign.

lessons.title: Vijayanagara, the Marathas and the Bhakti–Sufi traditions

story.title: Kabir's dohas in Neel's music class

scenes.text: In Varanasi, Neel's music teacher, Ustad Rafiq, teaches the class a doha by Kabir.
'Kabir was a weaver,' he says. 'He questioned empty rituals of all religions and spoke of one God within everyone.'
Neel's friend Gurleen says, 'Some of Kabir's verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib too!' The class realises how these traditions connected people across lines.

steps.title: The Vijayanagara empire
steps.body:
- Founded in **1336** by the brothers **Harihara and Bukka**, with the capital **Vijayanagara** (its ruins are at **Hampi**, Karnataka — a UNESCO World Heritage Site).
- **Krishnadeva Raya** (ruled 1509–1529) was its most famous ruler, known for building temples and gopurams and for his writing in Telugu.
- It competed with the **Bahmani** kingdom and later the Deccan Sultanates, who defeated it at the **Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi) in 1565**.
- Foreign visitors, including Portuguese travellers, described its wealthy markets.

steps.title: The Marathas and other regional powers
steps.body:
In the 17th century, **Shivaji** built a strong Maratha kingdom in the western Deccan, using forts and mobile cavalry. He was crowned in **1674**. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, Maratha power expanded under the **Peshwas**.

Other strong regional powers of the 18th century included **Hyderabad**, **Awadh** and **Bengal**, and the **Sikhs** in Punjab, who had organised themselves into bands (**jathas**) and later a kingdom under **Maharaja Ranjit Singh**.

steps.title: Bhakti and Sufi traditions
steps.body:
**Bhakti** means devotion — a personal, loving relationship with God, open to everyone regardless of caste or gender.
- In the south, the **Nayanars** (devotees of Shiva) and **Alvars** (devotees of Vishnu) composed Tamil hymns.
- Later saints include **Basavanna** (Karnataka), **Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram** (Maharashtra), **Mirabai** (Rajasthan), **Kabir** and **Surdas**.
- **Guru Nanak** (1469–1539) founded **Sikhism** at Kartarpur, teaching worship of one God, equality and honest work; his teachings are in the **Guru Granth Sahib**.

**Sufis** were Muslim mystics who stressed love of God and compassion. **Sufi khanqahs** (lodges) and **dargahs** (shrines), like that of **Nizamuddin Auliya** in Delhi and **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti** in Ajmer, attracted people of all faiths. **Qawwali** music grew from this tradition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking these movements were only about religion — they also questioned caste and ritual and used local languages, which shaped Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Punjabi and other literatures.
- Mixing up Hampi (ruins) and Vijayanagara (the historical city name) — they're the same place in different times.

lessons.title: Globes, maps, latitudes and longitudes

scenes.text: At 8:30 p.m. in Pune, Anaya video-calls her cousin Riya in London. Riya answers sleepily from school — it's only 3 p.m. there.
Anaya spins her globe. London sits on the 0° line of longitude; India's time is based on 82½° E.
82½ degrees × 4 minutes = 330 minutes = 5½ hours. India is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of London's standard time. Maths explains the sleepy cousin!

steps.title: Globe and the grid
steps.body:
A **globe** is a small model of the Earth. It is tilted because the Earth's **axis** is tilted (about 23½° from the vertical).

Imaginary lines help us locate places:
- **Latitudes (parallels):** circles running east–west, measured in degrees **north or south of the Equator (0°)**, up to 90° N and 90° S (the **poles**).
- **Longitudes (meridians):** half-circles from pole to pole, measured **east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°)**, which passes through **Greenwich** near London, up to 180°.

Together they form a **grid**. Any place can be described as, e.g., Delhi ≈ 28.6° N, 77.2° E.

steps.title: Important latitudes and heat zones
steps.body:
- **Equator** 0° — divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres
- **Tropic of Cancer** 23½° N — passes through the middle of India (e.g. Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, West Bengal and more)
- **Tropic of Capricorn** 23½° S
- **Arctic Circle** 66½° N; **Antarctic Circle** 66½° S

**Heat zones:** **Torrid** (between the tropics, the Sun is overhead at least once a year — hottest), **Temperate** (between the tropics and the circles), **Frigid** (inside the Arctic/Antarctic circles — coldest).

steps.title: Longitude and time
steps.body:
Earth turns **360° in 24 hours**, so **15° = 1 hour** and **1° = 4 minutes**. Places to the **east** are **ahead** in time.

**Indian Standard Time (IST)** is based on **82½° E** (passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh). 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes, so **IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min**.

Example: when it is noon at Greenwich (0°), at 45° E it is 45 × 4 = 180 min = 3 h ahead → **3 p.m.**; at 30° W it is 2 h behind → **10 a.m.**

Large countries like the USA and Russia use several time zones.

steps.title: Reading maps
steps.body:
A **map** is a drawing of all or part of the Earth on a flat surface. Three components:
- **Distance (scale):** e.g. 1 cm = 10 km.
- **Direction:** the four **cardinal directions** N, S, E, W and intermediate ones (NE, SE, SW, NW). Most maps have north at the top and an arrow marked N.
- **Symbols:** conventional symbols and colours — blue for water, green for plains/forests, brown for mountains, yellow for plateaus.

**Physical maps** show natural features; **political maps** show countries, states and cities; **thematic maps** show one topic (rainfall, population). A **sketch** is drawn from memory without scale; a **plan** is a large-scale drawing of a small area (like a house).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up latitude and longitude — memory tip: lat**itude** lines lie **flat** like the rungs of a ladder (ladder-tude).
- Forgetting that places **east** are **ahead** in time.
- Thinking flat maps show sizes perfectly — every flat world map distorts something (Greenland often looks far bigger than it really is).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. When it is 6 a.m. at Greenwich, what is the time in India (IST)?
2. A place is at 60° W. When it is noon at Greenwich, what is the time there?
3. Use the map-skills lab to find a place at 20° N, 80° E.

*Answers:* 1) 11:30 a.m. 2) 8 a.m. 3) In central India (Maharashtra–Chhattisgarh region)
