lessons.title: Motions of the Earth and seasons

story.title: Midnight sun for Ole, monsoon for Asha

scenes.text: In June, Ole in northern Norway sends Asha in Kerala a photo: the Sun still shining at midnight.
Asha replies with a photo of heavy monsoon rain. 'And my cousin in Melbourne, Australia, says it's winter there!'
How can one day in June be summer, winter and 'midnight sun' all at once? The answer: Earth's tilt as it travels around the Sun.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.body:
**Rotation** is Earth spinning on its **axis**, from **west to east**. One rotation takes about **24 hours**.

Effects:
- **Day and night** — the half facing the Sun has day; the other half has night. The line between them is the **circle of illumination**.
- The Sun appears to **rise in the east** and set in the west.

If Earth didn't rotate, one side would always be extremely hot and the other extremely cold.

steps.title: Revolution and the tilt
steps.body:
**Revolution** is Earth's movement **around the Sun** in a slightly oval path (**orbit**). One revolution takes about **365¼ days**. Every fourth year, the extra quarter-days add up to one day — **29 February** in a **leap year** (366 days).

Earth's axis is **tilted** (about 23½° from the perpendicular, making 66½° with the plane of the orbit) and always points the same way in space. So for part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, and for part it leans away.

steps.title: Solstices and equinoxes
steps.body:
- **21 June — summer solstice** (Northern Hemisphere): Sun overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**; longest day in the north. Areas inside the Arctic Circle get continuous daylight for some time around this date (the 'midnight sun'). It is **winter** in the Southern Hemisphere.
- **22 December — winter solstice** (Northern Hemisphere): Sun overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn**; shortest day in the north, summer in Australia.
- **21 March and 23 September — equinoxes:** Sun overhead at the **Equator**; day and night are roughly equal everywhere.

(Dates can vary by a day from year to year.)

steps.title: The biggest myth
steps.body:
**Myth:** 'Summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun.'
**Fact:** Seasons are caused by the **tilt**. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early **January** — during the Northern Hemisphere's winter!

India's **monsoon** season is a pattern of winds and rain, explained in the climate lesson; it isn't one of the four 'tilt' seasons.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a dark room, shine a torch (the Sun) on a tilted ball or orange with a stick through it (the Earth). Walk the ball in a circle around the torch, keeping the stick pointing the same way. Watch which half gets more direct light at each position.

statements.s: Earth rotates from west to east.
statements.why: That's why the Sun appears to rise in the east.

statements.s: Seasons happen because Earth is sometimes much closer to the Sun.
statements.why: The tilt of the axis causes seasons.

statements.s: On 21 June the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.
statements.why: Summer solstice in the north.

statements.s: A leap year has 366 days.
statements.why: An extra day, 29 February.

statements.s: When it is summer in India, it is summer in Australia too.
statements.why: The hemispheres have opposite seasons.

quiz.q: One rotation of Earth takes about
quiz.why: The Earth completes one rotation on its axis in about 24 hours, which makes one day.

quiz.q: Day and night are caused by
quiz.why: Day and night are caused by the rotation of the Earth, which turns different parts toward and away from the Sun. Revolution causes seasons.

quiz.q: Equinoxes occur around
quiz.why: The equinoxes, when day and night are equal, occur around 21 March and 23 September, when the Sun is overhead at the Equator.

quiz.q: The main cause of seasons is
quiz.why: Seasons are caused mainly by the tilt of Earth's axis, which changes how directly sunlight falls on each hemisphere during revolution.

lessons.title: Inside the Earth: rocks and landforms

story.title: Pemba and the river that carves

scenes.text: Pemba, from Sikkim, travels with his father to visit relatives in the Sundarbans of West Bengal.
In the mountains, the Teesta rushes through deep V-shaped valleys. On the plains, rivers wander in wide loops.
At the coast, the river splits into many channels, forming a delta of islands and mangroves. 'The same water that carves the mountains builds this land,' his father says.

steps.title: Earth's layers
steps.body:
- **Crust** — the thin outer layer we live on. About **35 km** thick under continents and only about **5 km** under oceans. Rich in silica and aluminium.
- **Mantle** — below the crust, extending to a depth of about 2,900 km. Very hot; parts move slowly.
- **Core** — the innermost layer, mostly **nickel and iron**; extremely hot.

The deepest mine and borehole reach only a few kilometres — we learn about deeper layers mainly from **earthquake waves**.

steps.title: Rocks and minerals
steps.body:
- **Igneous rocks** form when molten **magma** (inside Earth) or **lava** (on the surface) cools — **granite** (cools slowly inside), **basalt** (cools quickly on the surface; the Deccan plateau has a lot of it).
- **Sedimentary rocks** form from layers of small pieces (**sediments**) pressed together — sandstone, limestone. They may contain **fossils**.
- **Metamorphic rocks** form when rocks change under great heat and pressure — clay → slate; limestone → **marble** (the Taj Mahal is made of marble).

The **rock cycle**: rocks keep changing from one type to another over very long times.

steps.title: Forces that shape the land
steps.body:
**Inside forces (endogenic):** movement of **lithospheric plates** causes **earthquakes**, **volcanoes** and mountain-building. The Himalayas are young **fold mountains** still rising slowly as plates push together.

**Outside forces (exogenic):** **weathering** (breaking of rocks) and **erosion** (wearing away by water, wind, ice and waves), followed by **deposition**.

**Landforms:**
- Rivers: **waterfalls**, **meanders** (loops), **ox-bow lakes**, **flood plains**, **deltas** (the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is one of the world's largest)
- Sea waves: **sea caves**, **arches**, **stacks**, **beaches**
- Glaciers: deep valleys and **moraines** (deposited debris)
- Wind (deserts): **mushroom rocks**, **sand dunes**, **loess**

The three main landforms: **mountains**, **plateaus** (raised flat land, e.g. the Deccan, Chota Nagpur), **plains** (flat, fertile, often river-made — most densely populated).

steps.title: Earthquake safety
steps.body:
**Drop, Cover, Hold On:** get under a sturdy table, protect your head and neck, hold on until shaking stops. Stay away from windows, shelves and lifts. If outside, move to an open area away from buildings, trees and power lines. Call **112** in an emergency.

Common mistake: running out of a building while it is shaking — falling objects near exits cause many injuries.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pour a jug of water slowly down a slope of sand or soil in a tray. Watch for channels (valleys), loops (meanders) and a fan of deposits where the water stops (like a delta). Sketch what you see.

activity.prompt: Match the landform to what made it.

quiz.q: The innermost layer of Earth is the
quiz.why: The innermost layer of the Earth is the core, made mainly of nickel and iron. The crust is the outermost layer.

quiz.q: Marble is a
quiz.why: Marble is a metamorphic rock that forms from limestone under heat and pressure. Sedimentary and igneous rocks are formed differently.

quiz.q: Fossils are usually found in
quiz.why: Fossils are found in sedimentary rocks, because the remains of dead plants and animals get buried in layers of sediment. Heat in igneous rock destroys them.

quiz.q: The Himalayas are
quiz.why: The Himalayas are young fold mountains, formed when plates pushed together and crumpled the land. They are still rising.

quiz.q: During an earthquake indoors, you should
options: run down the stairs while shaking
quiz.why: During an earthquake indoors, drop to the floor, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on. Do not use lifts or stand near windows.

lessons.title: Air, water, climate and resources

story.title: The dried-up lake in Sunil's village

scenes.text: Sunil's grandmother in a village near Bengaluru remembers swimming in the village lake. Now it is mostly dry and full of plastic.
Sunil's school starts a project: clean the lake, desilt it with the panchayat's help, and dig rainwater pits.
After two monsoons, the lake holds water again and birds return. Sunil realises water is a renewable resource — but only if we look after it.

steps.title: The atmosphere
steps.body:
Air is a mixture of gases: **nitrogen ≈ 78%**, **oxygen ≈ 21%**, and about 1% others — argon, **carbon dioxide** (about 0.04%), water vapour, and dust.

Layers (from the ground up): **troposphere** (where weather happens, about 13 km on average), **stratosphere** (has the **ozone layer**, which absorbs harmful UV rays; aircraft often fly in its lower part), **mesosphere** (meteors burn up), **thermosphere**, **exosphere**.

**Weather** is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere; **climate** is the average weather of a place over many years (often 30 or more).

steps.title: The water cycle and oceans
steps.body:
About **97%** of Earth's water is **salty** ocean water. Only a small share is fresh water, and most of that is locked in ice caps and glaciers or underground.

**Water cycle:**
1. **Evaporation** — the Sun heats water; it becomes vapour
2. **Condensation** — vapour cools into tiny droplets → **clouds**
3. **Precipitation** — rain, snow, hail
4. **Run-off and infiltration** — water flows into rivers and seeps into the ground (groundwater) and returns to the sea

**Ocean movements:** **waves** (mainly by wind), **tides** (rise and fall of sea level twice a day, caused by the gravitational pull of the **Moon** and the Sun), and **ocean currents** (warm and cold streams of water).

steps.title: Natural vegetation and resources
steps.body:
Vegetation depends on rainfall and temperature: **tropical evergreen** forests (heavy rain, e.g. Western Ghats, North-East), **tropical deciduous** forests (shed leaves in dry season — teak, sal), **thorny bushes** (dry areas of Rajasthan), **mangroves** (salty coastal swamps — Sundarbans), **mountain vegetation**.

**Resources:**
- **Renewable** (replenished naturally): solar and wind energy, water, forests (if not overused)
- **Non-renewable** (limited stock): coal, petroleum, natural gas, many minerals
- Also: **natural**, **human-made** (buildings, machines) and **human resources** (people's skills and knowledge)

**Sustainable development:** using resources carefully so that future generations also have enough. Reduce, reuse, recycle.

steps.title: Pollution and conservation
steps.body:
- **Air pollution:** vehicle and factory smoke, crop burning, dust → breathing problems, smog. Rising **greenhouse gases** like carbon dioxide are warming the planet (**global warming / climate change**).
- **Water pollution:** sewage, chemicals, plastic.

**What you can do:** save water, plant and protect trees, segregate waste, avoid single-use plastic, walk or cycle short distances, switch off unused lights. **Rainwater harvesting** helps refill groundwater.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up **weather** (today) and **climate** (long-term average).
- Thinking the ozone layer is in the troposphere — it's in the **stratosphere**.
- Calling forests 'unlimited' — renewable resources can still run out if used faster than they regrow.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Run the water-cycle lab and change the temperature and wind. Then do a one-week water audit at home: list every use of water and find two ways to save at least 10 litres a day.

courses.title: Our Democracy: the Constitution, Parliament and local government
courses.summary: Why India has a Constitution, what the Preamble promises, our Fundamental Rights and Duties, how Parliament makes laws, how courts protect rights, and how Gram Panchayats and municipalities run our villages and cities.
outcomes: Learners can explain why a constitution is needed and what the Preamble says
Learners can list the Fundamental Rights and some Fundamental Duties

Learners can describe rural and urban local government and how citizens take part
Learners can apply ideas of equality and rights to real-life situations

lessons.title: The Constitution and the Preamble

scenes.text: On 26 November — Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) — Nandini's school in Raipur gathers to read the Preamble aloud.
Her friend Imran whispers, 'Why do we need a 'rule book' for a whole country?' Nandini isn't sure.
Their teacher, Ms Gill, asks them to play a game with no rules. Within minutes, there are arguments. 'That,' she smiles, 'is why a country needs a Constitution.'

steps.title: What a constitution does
steps.body:
A **constitution** is the **supreme law** of a country. It:
- sets out the **ideals** the country wants to live by
- decides **how the government is formed** and what powers it has
- puts **limits** on those powers so leaders can't misuse them
- protects the **rights** of citizens, especially minorities

All other laws must follow the Constitution. A law that goes against it can be struck down by the courts.

steps.title: How India's Constitution was made
steps.body:
- It was written by the **Constituent Assembly**, which met from December 1946.
- **Dr B. R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee** and is often called the chief architect of the Constitution.
- It was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now celebrated as **Constitution Day**) and **came into force on 26 January 1950** (**Republic Day**).
- It is one of the **longest written constitutions** in the world.
- It can be changed by **amendments** passed by Parliament following a special procedure.

steps.title: The Preamble
steps.body:
The **Preamble** is the introduction to the Constitution. It begins 'We, the people of India…' — meaning power comes from the people.

It describes India as a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic** ('socialist' and 'secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976):
- **Sovereign** — India makes its own decisions; no outside power controls it
- **Socialist** — reducing inequality of wealth and opportunity
- **Secular** — the state treats all religions equally and has no official religion
- **Democratic** — people elect their governments
- **Republic** — the head of state (the President) is elected, not a hereditary monarch

It promises citizens **Justice** (social, economic, political), **Liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), **Equality** (of status and opportunity) and **Fraternity** (brotherhood/sisterhood, assuring dignity and unity).

steps.title: Fundamental Rights
steps.body:
The Constitution guarantees six groups of **Fundamental Rights**:
1. **Right to Equality** — equal before the law; no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; **untouchability is abolished** (Article 17)
2. **Right to Freedom** — of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession; protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21)
3. **Right against Exploitation** — bans trafficking, forced labour, and employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work
4. **Right to Freedom of Religion**
5. **Cultural and Educational Rights** — minorities can protect their language and culture and set up educational institutions
6. **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (Article 32) — you can go to court if your rights are violated. Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

The **Right to Education** (Article 21A, added in 2002) gives children aged **6–14** the right to free and compulsory education.

steps.title: Fundamental Duties and closing note
steps.body:
Rights come with responsibilities. **Fundamental Duties** (Article 51A, added in 1976) include: respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem; protecting the environment; developing a scientific temper; protecting public property; promoting harmony; and (for parents/guardians) providing opportunities for education to children aged 6–14.

*This is general education, not legal advice.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the dates: **adopted 26 Nov 1949**, **in force 26 Jan 1950**.
- Thinking Fundamental Rights are unlimited — they have reasonable limits (e.g. free speech does not allow inciting violence).
- 'Secular' does not mean anti-religion — it means the state is **neutral** and treats all religions equally.

A feeling of brotherhood and unity

quiz.q: The Constitution came into force on
quiz.why: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day. It was adopted on 26 November 1949.

quiz.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee?
quiz.why: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, so he is called the architect of the Constitution.

quiz.q: Which right lets you go to court if your rights are violated?
quiz.why: The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets you approach the courts if your rights are violated. It is under Article 32.

quiz.q: Untouchability is abolished under the
quiz.why: Untouchability is abolished by Article 17, which is part of the Right to Equality. It makes the practice of untouchability a punishable offence.

quiz.q: The Right to Education covers children aged
quiz.why: The Right to Education covers children aged 6–14 years and provides free and compulsory education under Article 21A.

lessons.title: Parliament, government and courts

scenes.text: Aditya's elder sister Priyanka in Lucknow just turned 18 and votes for the first time in the Lok Sabha election. Her finger gets a mark of indelible ink.
A few months later, Aditya watches a debate on TV about a new bill in Parliament. MPs argue, ask questions and finally vote.
Then a citizens' group challenges a rule in the Supreme Court. Aditya realises: people elect law-makers, Parliament makes laws, and courts check that laws follow the Constitution.

steps.title: Parliament
steps.body:
India's **Parliament** = the **President** + the **Lok Sabha** (House of the People) + the **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States).
- **Lok Sabha** members (**MPs**) are **directly elected** by citizens aged **18 and above**, usually every **5 years**. India is divided into **constituencies**; each elects one MP. The candidate with the most votes wins.
- **Rajya Sabha** members are elected mainly by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (MLAs). Members serve 6-year terms; about one-third retire every two years. The President nominates 12 members with special knowledge.

Parliament's jobs: **make laws**, **control the government** (questions, debates, approval of the budget) and **represent** the people.

steps.title: The executive
steps.body:
- The party or coalition with a **majority** in the Lok Sabha forms the government. Its leader becomes the **Prime Minister**, who chooses the **Council of Ministers**.
- The **President** is the constitutional head of state; in most matters the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
- The **opposition** questions and criticises the government — an essential part of democracy.
- In the states, **MLAs** are elected to the Legislative Assembly; the government is led by the **Chief Minister**, and the **Governor** is the constitutional head.

steps.title: How a bill becomes a law
steps.body:
1. A **bill** (proposed law) is introduced in either House (money bills only in the Lok Sabha).
2. It is debated and may be sent to a committee for detailed study.
3. It is voted on and passed by the first House.
4. The second House debates and passes it.
5. The **President** gives assent — it becomes an **Act** (law).

Citizens also influence laws through the media, petitions, peaceful protests and public consultations.

steps.title: The judiciary
steps.body:
Courts settle disputes, protect Fundamental Rights and check that laws follow the Constitution (**judicial review**).
- **Structure:** **Supreme Court** (New Delhi, highest court) → **High Courts** (in states) → **District Courts** and lower courts.
- The judiciary is **independent** — the government cannot control its decisions.
- **Public Interest Litigation (PIL):** a person or group can approach the High Court or Supreme Court on behalf of those whose rights are violated.

India's main criminal laws today are the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam**, in force from **1 July 2024**.

*This is general education, not legal advice.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Prime Minister is directly elected by all citizens — voters elect MPs; the majority's leader becomes PM.
- Confusing MP (Parliament) with MLA (state assembly).
- Thinking the President makes laws alone — Parliament passes them; the President gives assent.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Hold a class 'mock Parliament' on a school rule (e.g. 'no homework on weekends'). Introduce the bill, debate, vote, and let the principal be the 'President' who gives assent. What did you learn about compromise?

activity.prompt: Put the stages of a bill becoming a law in order.
items: A bill is introduced in one House of Parliament
Members debate it and a committee may examine it
The first House votes and passes it
The second House debates and passes it
The President gives assent
It becomes an Act (law)

quiz.q: The minimum voting age in India is
quiz.why: The minimum voting age in India is 18 years. Any citizen who is 18 or older can vote.

quiz.q: The Prime Minister is
options: the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha
quiz.why: The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha. The PM is not directly elected by all citizens.

quiz.q: The highest court in India is the
quiz.why: The Supreme Court in New Delhi is the highest court in India. High Courts and District Courts are below it.

quiz.q: A bill becomes an Act after
options: both Houses pass it and the President assents
quiz.why: A bill becomes an Act after both Houses of Parliament pass it and the President gives assent. One House alone is not enough.

quiz.q: India's main criminal code in force from 1 July 2024 is the
quiz.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code as India's main criminal code from 1 July 2024.

lessons.title: Local government: panchayats and municipalities

scenes.text: In Hardas village, Madhya Pradesh, the only handpump near the school has been broken for weeks. Students like Ravi walk far for water.
At the Gram Sabha meeting, Ravi's mother, Kamla Devi, stands up and raises the issue. Other villagers agree.
The Sarpanch, Mrs Bano, and the panchayat secretary record it. Within a month, the handpump is repaired with panchayat funds. Ordinary people can make government work.

steps.title: Why local government?
steps.body:
Many problems — water, roads, street lights, drains, local schools and health centres — are best solved **close to the people**. So India has three levels of government: **national (Union)**, **state**, and **local**.

The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave rural local bodies (**Panchayati Raj**) constitutional status, and the **74th Amendment (1992)** did the same for urban local bodies. At least **one-third of seats** in these bodies are reserved for **women** (many states reserve 50%), and seats are also reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

steps.title: Panchayati Raj (villages)
steps.body:
Three tiers (in most states):
1. **Gram Panchayat** — village level. Headed by the **Sarpanch** (or Pradhan), with elected **ward members (Panch)**. A **secretary**, appointed by the government, keeps records.
2. **Panchayat Samiti** (Block level)
3. **Zila Parishad** (District level)

The **Gram Sabha** is the meeting of **all adults (18+) who live in the village and are voters**. It approves plans, checks the panchayat's work and spending, and keeps it accountable. Members are elected for **5 years**.

Panchayats raise money from local taxes (on houses, markets) and receive funds from state and central governments.

steps.title: Urban local bodies (towns and cities)
steps.body:
- **Municipal Corporation** — big cities (e.g. Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru)
- **Municipal Council (Nagar Palika)** — smaller towns
- **Nagar Panchayat** — areas changing from rural to urban

The city is divided into **wards**, each electing a **councillor**. Councillors decide on budgets and issues; the **Mayor** heads the corporation (in most cities). The **Municipal Commissioner** (a government officer) and administrative staff carry out decisions.

Services: water supply, garbage collection, drains and sewers, street lights, roads, parks, hospitals, schools, birth and death certificates. Money comes from **property tax**, other local taxes and government grants.

steps.title: How citizens can take part
steps.body:
- **Attend** Gram Sabha or ward meetings and raise issues.
- **Complain** through municipal helplines, apps or websites (keep a complaint number).
- **Use the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005** to ask for information on public works and spending.
- **Vote** in local elections — turnout matters.
- **Pay** local taxes and follow rules (e.g. waste segregation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the **Gram Sabha** (all adult voters) with the **Gram Panchayat** (elected body).
- Thinking the Mayor is a national leader — the Mayor heads a city corporation.
- Thinking only adults can make a difference — students can raise issues through school, parents and youth groups.

a.text: Garbage has piled up at the corner of your street in a city for two weeks. It smells and attracts flies. What do you do first?

choices.label: Burn the garbage
choices.feedback: Burning waste releases toxic smoke and is often prohibited.

choices.label: With a parent, register a complaint with the municipal helpline or app
choices.feedback: Right — the municipality is responsible for garbage collection.

b.text: Neighbours cough from the smoke and the pile returns in days. What next?

choices.label: Complain to the municipality and inform the ward councillor
choices.feedback: Go to the body responsible.

choices.label: Just ignore it
choices.feedback: The problem won't fix itself.

c.text: You have a complaint number, but nothing happens for 5 days. What now?

choices.label: Contact your ward councillor with the complaint number, and get neighbours to sign a joint letter
choices.feedback: Elected representatives must respond; collective action helps.

choices.label: Post angry insults about officials online
choices.feedback: Insults rarely help; clear facts and follow-up do.

end1.text: The councillor follows up; a regular collection point and schedule are set. You also start segregating wet and dry waste at home. Active, polite, persistent citizens make local government work!

end2.text: Key idea: know which body is responsible (here the municipality), use official channels, keep records, follow up with your elected representative, and work with neighbours.

quiz.q: The Gram Sabha consists of
options: all adult voters of the village
quiz.why: The Gram Sabha is made up of all adult voters of the village, who meet to discuss village matters. It is not only elected members.

quiz.q: The head of a Gram Panchayat is the
quiz.why: The head of a Gram Panchayat is the Sarpanch (called Pradhan in some states). A Collector is a district officer.

quiz.q: Which amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj?
quiz.why: The 73rd Amendment of 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj. The 74th did the same for urban local bodies.

quiz.q: A big city is governed by a
quiz.why: A big city is governed by a Municipal Corporation, with elected councillors and a mayor. A Gram Panchayat is for villages.

quiz.q: At least what share of seats in local bodies is reserved for women?
quiz.why: At least one-third of seats in local bodies like panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, and many states give 50%. It is neither all nor none.

lessons.title: Equality, diversity and standing up for rights

story.title: The water pot at Omprakash's school

scenes.text: Long ago, in some places, children from certain castes were not allowed to drink from the same water pot as others. Dr Ambedkar faced this as a schoolboy.
Today, in Class 7 in Jaipur, Omprakash notices a new boy, Sadiq, being left out at lunch because he speaks Hindi with a different accent.
Omprakash sits with Sadiq, and soon others join. 'Equality isn't just a law,' says their teacher Ms Rathore. 'It's what we do every day.'

steps.title: Equality in a democracy
steps.body:
In India, **every adult has one vote**, whatever their wealth, caste, religion or gender — this is **universal adult franchise**. The Constitution says all persons are **equal before the law** (Article 14).

But equality on paper is not enough. People may still face **discrimination** — being treated unfairly because of caste, religion, gender, disability, language, appearance or economic background.

**Prejudice** = judging people negatively without knowing them. **Stereotype** = fixing people into one image ('girls are bad at maths', 'boys don't cry'). Both can lead to discrimination.

steps.title: Unity in diversity
steps.body:
India has many languages, religions, foods, festivals, clothes and ways of life. **Diversity** enriches us; it can also be used to divide people.

The Constitution protects diversity through rights to religion, culture and education, and promotes **fraternity**. Freedom-struggle leaders from every region and community fought together; the national song and the national anthem were written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Rabindranath Tagore respectively.

steps.title: Steps that promote equality
steps.body:
- **Laws:** untouchability abolished; laws against caste atrocities; equal pay rules; laws protecting the rights of persons with disabilities.
- **Government schemes:** e.g. the **midday meal** scheme (PM-POSHAN), which also helps children of all backgrounds sit and eat together.
- **Reservations** in education, jobs and legislatures for historically disadvantaged groups.
- **People's movements and media** that raise voices against injustice.
- **Everyday choices:** including others, calling out unfair jokes, using respectful language.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'treating everyone exactly the same' always means fairness — sometimes extra support (like ramps for wheelchair users) is needed so that everyone has an **equal opportunity**.
- Thinking discrimination is only big events — small daily exclusions hurt too.
- Assuming one person can't help — standing with someone often encourages others.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write down one stereotype you have heard about a group. Find one real person (from news, books or your life) who breaks it. What would you say next time you hear that stereotype?

activity.prompt: Think of a time you felt left out or saw someone else being excluded. What happened, how did it feel, and what could you (or others) have done differently?
activity.hint: Be honest — this note stays private on your device. Try to name one small action you can take this week to include someone.

quiz.q: Universal adult franchise means
options: every adult citizen has one vote
quiz.why: Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen has one vote, whatever their wealth, gender, caste or education. It rules out voting only for the rich, men or graduates.

quiz.q: 'Girls can't play cricket' is an example of a
quiz.why: 'Girls can't play cricket' is a stereotype, a fixed and unfair idea about a group of people. It is not a fact, law or right, and it limits opportunity.

quiz.q: A ramp for wheelchair users is an example of
quiz.why: A ramp gives wheelchair users the same chance to enter a building, so it provides equal opportunity. Discrimination would be to leave them out.

quiz.q: Article 14 of the Constitution is about
quiz.why: Article 14 gives equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to all persons. It does not deal with duties, local government or the right to vote.

questions.q: Constitution Day is celebrated on
questions.why: Constitution Day is celebrated on 26 November because the Constitution was adopted on that day in 1949. 26 January is Republic Day, when it came into force.

questions.q: MPs of the Lok Sabha are elected
questions.why: Lok Sabha MPs are elected directly by voters aged 18 and above in each constituency. The President, MLAs and judges do not elect them.

questions.q: The head of a Gram Panchayat is the
questions.why: The head of a Gram Panchayat is the Sarpanch. A Mayor heads a city corporation, and the Chief Minister heads a state government.

questions.q: 'Secular' in the Preamble means
options: the state treats all religions equally
the state has an official religion
questions.why: 'Secular' means the state treats all religions equally and has no official religion. It does not ban religion or allow only one.

questions.q: Which is a Fundamental Right?
options: Right to vote in another country
questions.why: The Right to Equality is one of the six Fundamental Rights. The others listed, like a free car or skipping school, are not rights in the Constitution.

questions.q: Garbage collection in a city is mainly the job of the
questions.why: Collecting garbage in a city is a service of the urban local body, the Municipal Corporation. The Gram Sabha is for villages, and the Rajya Sabha and Supreme Court have other roles.

questions.q: The President of India gives assent to a bill
questions.why: A bill becomes law only after both Houses pass it and then the President gives assent. Assent is the final stage of law-making.

questions.q: The Gram Sabha's key role is to
options: check and approve the panchayat's work
questions.why: The Gram Sabha checks and approves the panchayat's work and its budget, so villagers can hold it accountable. It does not collect income tax or run the police.

questions.q: Public Interest Litigation allows
options: anyone to file a case on behalf of people whose rights are violated
the PM to make laws alone
foreign courts to decide Indian cases
questions.why: A Public Interest Litigation lets any person file a case on behalf of people whose rights are violated, so it widens access to justice.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: It was adopted on 26 Nov 1949 and came into force on 26 Jan 1950
It came into force on 15 Aug 1947
The Constitution came into force on 26 Nov 1949

questions.q: Which group of Fundamental Rights did Dr Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.why: Dr Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution, because Article 32 lets citizens go to court to enforce all their other rights.

questions.q: Why is an independent judiciary important?
options: So the police can decide cases
So judges can make all laws
So courts can check government and protect rights without pressure
questions.why: An independent judiciary can check the government and protect people's rights without pressure from it. It doesn't replace elections, the police or lawmaking.
